communities.name: Copyright notices and interview title pages
communities.narrative: This cluster is not a story the musicians tell but the front matter of their transcripts. Almost every segment, drawn from 67 different interviews and overwhelmingly from the Rutgers Institute of Jazz Studies, opens with the standard IJS copyright warning. Most then carry the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project title page, naming the interviewee, the interviewer, the date and the reel or tape number. Many continue into the interviewer's spoken opening: a recorder or microphone check, a date and place announcement, and a first question about birth or parents. The recurring interviewers are Patricia Willard, Helen Oakley Dance, Stanley Dance and Milt Hinton, with interviews recorded in places such as Washington, New York, Los Angeles and Paris. The interviews span the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s. The samples differ only in how much of the opening they take in. A few add small asides, such as Clayton's green-ink corrections, an editor's note, or a caller asking about copying Tulane's records. None of the samples holds a musician's own account of events.

communities.name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years
communities.narrative: This is the large shared story of military service in the 1940s: being drafted or enlisting, passing or dodging the induction physical, and then serving, very often as a musician. Most tellers are set between about 1918 and 1951, with the bulk in World War II (1942-46). Their stories centre on Navy bands at Great Lakes, Army and Air Corps bands at Fort Dix, Fort Lee, Greensboro and Fort Huachuca, and USO or ENSA shows for troops in England, Normandy and the Pacific. Tellers agree that a horn could shape where you were sent, and that military life was a school of discipline and big-band playing. They differ on how it felt: some say they loved Army life, while others describe boredom, going AWOL, or combat close calls such as being strafed on Christmas Day 1944. Race runs through many accounts, including segregated bands and units, being turned away because they were Black, and encounters with white soldiers. Others tell of avoiding service through eyesight, age, a faked injury or a lost draft card, or of resuming careers with Basie, Calloway and others after discharge. The tellers are mostly Black and white sidemen and bandleaders, plus a few women and singers who entertained troops.

communities.name: Archive copyright notices and interviewee headnotes
communities.narrative: This is not a story the musicians tell but the boilerplate that opens each transcript. Nearly every segment, almost all from the Hamilton College (Fillius) collection, begins with the archive's copyright statement. It is followed by a short biographical note on the interviewee and the interview details: date, place, interviewer, and sometimes a Zoom setting or an event such as the Allegheny Jazz Party or a jazz cruise. Interviewers such as Monk Rowe and Michael Woods appear as the people introducing the session. The interviewees range from Rashied Ali, Toshiko Akiyoshi and Christian McBride to Flip Phillips and Al Grey, and there is no shared period or musical subject. The few outliers, such as the Alice Kern affidavit on Tiger Rag authorship and Sam Wooding's appended biography sheet, are also front-matter or reference material, not narrated memory. The cluster is useful mainly for finding where each interview starts.

communities.name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate
communities.narrative: This community is almost entirely the opening minutes of the Fillius Jazz Archive interviews at Hamilton College, mostly conducted by Monk Rowe (with Michael Woods in some). Nearly 400 of the 489 segments are tagged interview logistics, and about 430 different interviews contribute one each. The typical segment starts with the archive's copyright notice and a short biographical note, then the interviewer's welcome and introduction of the guest. Around that sit small bits of setting: the interview takes place in Clinton, Utica, New Hartford, a festival hotel or a musician's home, or, in later years, over Zoom. Some openings carry early small talk, such as a joke about a hat, an honor at a jazz party, a memorabilia-filled office, the word 'black' on tape, or how a guest describes himself at a cocktail party. A few openings also explain how Joe Williams and Milt Fillius started the archive. The tellers do not disagree, because this is the interviewer's framing rather than a story told by the musicians. Dates are mostly absent, and the stated period of 1960-2020 only reflects when the interviews were recorded.

communities.name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band
communities.narrative: This community gathers the stories musicians tell about Jelly Roll Morton, mostly from Tulane and Rutgers interviews. Nearly every segment is a portrait of one man, set between about 1905 and the early 1940s. Tellers who knew him in New Orleans remember a young pianist on Basin Street who traveled for gambling games and, in one account, had already played tunes like The Pearls as a boy on the Gulf Coast. Those who met him in Chicago and Harlem remember the diamonds, silk shirts and Lincolns, and the boasting. In the 1930s he held court on the corner outside the Harlem Rhythm Club, then worked at the Jungle Inn and led touring and rehearsal bands. Tellers disagree about his character and his music. Albert Nicholas and J. C. Higginbotham defend him as proud, truthful and funny. Others recall contempt for Tatum, Ellington and younger players, and some musicians who heard him later found his band dull or his solo piano quaint. A second strand concerns the work itself: the Red Hot Peppers records, his written parts and arrangements, session personnel, and who actually played with him. Sidemen such as Ed Garland, Walter P. Thomas, Happy Caldwell and Jacques Butler tell how he hired them.

communities.name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men
communities.narrative: This is the largest cluster of stories about Duke Ellington and his orchestra, told by roughly 217 interviewees, mostly from the 1930s to the 1960s. Duke Ellington is tagged in almost every segment, along with the band's central figures: Johnny Hodges, Billy Strayhorn, Harry Carney, Sonny Greer, Cootie Williams and Ben Webster. Alumni such as Barney Bigard, Quentin Jackson, Cootie Williams, Marshall Royal and Tom Whaley recount joining, subbing for or leaving the band, who sat in which chair, and what Duke was like as a bandleader and a person. Outsiders such as Charlie Barnet, Woody Herman, Milt Hinton and Helen Oakley Dance tell their own versions: sitting in, hiring Ellington sidemen for record dates, producing small-band sessions, and arguing over his music. The tellers agree that Ellington was in a class by himself as a composer and that he wrote for his players' individual voices. They differ on his character, which ranges from an affectionate, playful and tireless figure to an agitator who tested his men, and on how much credit Strayhorn received. Cotton Club, Apollo and Newport settings recur, with comparisons to Basie and Lunceford.

communities.name: Playing with and hearing Coltrane
communities.narrative: This community gathers the many stories musicians tell about John Coltrane, mostly set in the 1950s and 1960s in New York, Philadelphia and on the road. Bandmates such as Elvin Jones, McCoy Tyner and Roy Haynes describe the quartet from the inside: the quiet, unspoken way Coltrane led, the feeling of being "in the pocket", and the later split when Tyner and Jones left as the music moved toward free playing. Younger players and peers (Charles Lloyd, Pat LaBarbera, Chuck Mancuso, Cedar Walton) tell of hearing him live at the Five Spot, the Village Vanguard, the Jazz Workshop and the Village Theater, often seeing him practice obsessively. Others use him as a measuring stick for their own playing, as with Frank Foster on sheets of sound and Curtis Fuller calling him a guru. Tellers largely agree he was spiritual, relentless and a seeker, while a few dissent (Kenny Davern never cared for him). The edges of the cluster drift into the wider 1960s avant-garde, with Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, Eric Dolphy and the Lenox School dispute over playing without changes.

communities.name: Hunting for old band photographs and scrapbooks
communities.narrative: In this community the interview itself turns into a search for pictures. Interviewers, above all Bill Russell and the Tulane/Hogan Archive team, ask a musician whether any photographs, clippings or scrapbooks survive. The musician then looks through albums, sends for a scrapbook, or names a relative or acquaintance who might have a copy. The stories are mostly set in the 1910s to 1960s, with New Orleans at the centre and some Midwest and New York material. The recurring complaint is that early jazz bands were rarely photographed, and brass bands were photographed more often. Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit and Buddy Bolden are the most sought-after subjects. Some tellers have an item to lend or copy, such as Kid Thomas Valentine's band picture, Darnell Howard's only photograph of his Minneapolis band, and Papa Jack Laine's and Johnny DeDroit's scrapbooks. Others have lost theirs, as Bella Cornish lost her Bolden band photograph, or say they have none. A few later interviews outside New Orleans, with Benny Golson, Sheila Jordan and Melba Liston, repeat the pattern: identifying people in photographs, or regretting that no photographs or tapes were kept. Most of the segments are short logistical exchanges, and they are often about arranging to copy a picture.

communities.name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band
communities.narrative: This community gathers musicians' memories of Cannonball Adderley, with a smaller strand about Bill Evans, mostly set between the 1950s and 1970s. Most tellers are younger altoists, singers and drummers who heard him live, met him at a clinic, or took him as an influence. Many of these interviews are conducted by a host (Rowe) who plays or mentions Adderley records, so identifying his tone in a blindfold test and discussing albums such as Country Preacher, Big Man and Somewhere recur. Nearly everyone describes him the same way: warm, humble, intelligent, joyful, hospitable and a hearty eater, with a big alto sound, playing by ear and educating his audiences. Musicians who worked with or near him (Ernie Watts, Phil Woods, Kidd Jordan, Joe Williams, Terri Lyne Carrington) tell first-hand stories, while others speak as fans or influenced players. A secondary thread follows Bill Evans through Gunther Schuller hiring him, the Wagner sessions, his trio drum chair at the Vanguard, and his decline. The tellers agree on Adderley's character; they differ on whether his importance lies in his playing, his bands, or his personality.

communities.name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band
communities.narrative: This community collects stories from some 115 interviewees about working with, auditioning for, or simply encountering Miles Davis, whose name appears in nearly every segment. The period runs mainly from the late 1940s to the early 1970s, with outliers into the 1980s and 1990 when later sidemen such as Branford Marsalis and Rick Margitza tell their versions. Most scenes are set in New York (Birdland, the Village Vanguard, Cafe Bohemia, Small's Paradise) and in the Columbia studios. Many tellers recount being recruited, tested on the bandstand, or turned down, and what Miles paid and demanded. Others describe particular recording sessions (Kind of Blue, Bitches Brew, Live Evil, the 1950s sessions) and how Miles ran a studio, often with very little instruction or rehearsal. Members of the 1960s quintet, such as Jimmy Cobb and Ron Carter, and the electric-period players, such as Jack DeJohnette and Dave Liebman, give insider accounts. Sitters-in, peers and early acquaintances, such as Clark Terry on the young Miles in East St. Louis, supply outside views. The tellers differ mostly in era: the acoustic quintet players stress craft and swing, while the 1970s and later players stress open-ended vamps, electric instruments and Miles's cryptic leadership.

communities.name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader
communities.narrative: This community collects the stories that sidemen, arrangers and younger admirers tell about Benny Goodman, mostly as an employer and a personality. The tellers span the swing era through his last years: Eddie Sauter and Jerry Jerome from the late 1930s and early 40s, Slam Stewart, Ed Shaughnessy and Eddie Bert in the postwar bands, Phil Woods on the 1962 Russian tour, and Bucky Pizzarelli, Peter Appleyard, Doc Cheatham, Ken Peplowski and Loren Schoenberg from the 1970s and 80s. The core tale is of a driven, music-obsessed perfectionist, known for "the glare", firing players, switching tunes without warning, and forgetting names (the Terry Gibbs "Pops" and Ziggy Elman anecdotes). Tellers disagree on how to read him. Some call him mean or egomaniacal, others a perfect gentleman, generous to young players, loyal to his family, and ahead of his time in hiring Black musicians. Several speculate that his aloofness was self-protection. Around this core are stories of specific jobs, such as writing weekly charts for the band, sextet and bebop-era dates, tours of Japan and Russia, Las Vegas and Carnegie Hall, and comparisons with Artie Shaw, Teddy Wilson and Gene Krupa. A few stray segments about other drummers or recording hobbyists sit at the edges.

communities.name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: This community gathers the stories musicians tell about Thelonious Monk: hearing him, working with him, and learning to understand him. Set mostly between the 1940s and 1970s in New York, the stories centre on Minton's Playhouse in the early bebop years, then on the Five Spot, Village Vanguard and Village Gate. Sidemen and contemporaries such as Roy Haynes, Elvin Jones, Wilbur Ware and Howard McGhee describe his odd tempos, tricky tunes and unspoken demands in rehearsal and on the bandstand. Younger players including Chick Corea, George Benson, Charles Tolliver and Ellis Marsalis tell of coming late to his music, or of him as a mentor and an indispensable repertory. A second strand is personal anecdote: his silences, his dry humour (the tainted orange juice), the pie through the window, his mother, and Lorraine Gordon's early publicity efforts. The tellers broadly agree that his music looked simple but was hard to play or sing, and that he knew his own worth. They differ on whether sidemen found him difficult (Orrin Keepnews denies it) and on how quickly they came to appreciate him (Ramsey Lewis first thought he could not play). A few peripheral samples only mention Monk in passing, or concern other people named Monk.

communities.name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy
communities.narrative: This community gathers hundreds of stories, told by musicians in over 260 interviews across all four archives, in which Charlie Parker is the central figure. Most are set between about 1939 and 1951, in the places where Bird's career unfolded: Kansas City and the Jay McShann band, then New York (52nd Street, Minton's, Birdland, the Apollo), Chicago, Detroit and Los Angeles (Billy Berg's). The tellers are peers and sidemen (Buster Smith, Buddy Tate, Gene Ramey, Roy Haynes, Ray Brown, Howard McGhee, John Malachi), younger players who sat in with him or heard him as teenagers, and a few friends, critics and family contacts. They agree on his astonishing ear and playing, and that other players were awed by him. They differ on the person and the period. Some remember a young Parker still learning in Kansas City, some remember him at his peak with McShann or Eckstine, and others recall him in trouble, difficult or unreliable. Many stories also pull in Dizzy Gillespie and the wider bebop circle, and some drift to the tellers' own careers, with Parker only a passing mention.

communities.name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man
communities.narrative: Musicians from every generation and collection tell stories about Art Tatum, the nearly blind pianist whose playing awed and humbled other pianists. The earliest accounts are first-hearing stories set in the 1920s and early 1930s, in Columbus, Louisville, Toledo and Chicago. Vic Dickenson heard him as a teenager at the Ohio blind school, and Eddie Barefield turned back when Tatum opened with Tiger Rag. The central scene is the after-hours session or cutting contest, in Harlem, Cleveland and Los Angeles, where Tatum sat down after Fats Waller, Teddy Wilson or Oscar Peterson and wiped everyone out. A second strand is Tatum as a person. Tellers recall his beer drinking, pinochle and card memory, love of baseball and track meets, independence despite his blindness, and the drunken episode of driving a car. A smaller group of pianists and sidemen, among them Jimmy Rowles, Richard Wyands, Teddy Edwards, Gerald Wiggins and Red Callender, describe working opposite him or being encouraged by him. The tellers agree on his supremacy and his generosity to younger players. They differ on small points: Tiny Grimes thought he lacked showmanship, and Roy Eldridge doubted he was totally blind.

communities.name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Across nearly 400 interviews, musicians are asked about, or volunteer, the piano players they heard and worked with, and they answer with names, rankings and short portraits. The largest body of stories is set in New Orleans from the 1900s to the 1920s, where interviewers from Tulane's Hogan Archive press for pianists of the district and the dance halls: Steve Lewis, Tony Jackson, Walter Pichon, Helen Edwards, Dude Amaker and the Frazier brothers. Tellers describe who read music and who played by ear, who could transpose at sight, who won piano contests, and who played in the black keys or with their feet. A second strand moves to Chicago, New York and Kansas City, where horn players, singers and bandleaders talk about Earl Hines, Art Tatum, Fats Waller, James P. Johnson and Teddy Wilson as the standard others were measured against, and about stride and barrelhouse players. Tellers tend to agree on the great names and the sense that piano was the district's craft, but differ in whom they rank highest and how they describe style. Pianists such as Hank Jones, Horace Henderson and Ram Ramirez also talk about their own playing and their peers, and the cluster includes a few later and gospel-piano reflections.

communities.name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger
communities.narrative: Musicians across the country tell stories about the American Federation of Musicians and its locals, mostly set between the 1920s and the 1970s in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, New Orleans and the Bay Area. The commonest stories are about joining: getting a union card, passing (or not needing) an audition, paying initiation fees, and then waiting out transfer and residency rules when moving to a new city, as Art Hodes, Eddie Durham, John Best and David Spinozza describe. A second strand is enforcement and money: scale wages, fines for sitting in, bands limited by local rules, and the cards musicians used as identification against police harassment. The most heavily told story, especially by West Coast and New Orleans Black musicians such as Marshall Royal, Gerald Wilson, Benny Carter, Earl Watkins and Paul Howard, is the long fight to merge the segregated Black and white locals (767 into 47, Local 669 in Oakland, New Orleans Local 496), with Petrillo as a looming figure. Tellers agree the merger opened integrated bands and clubs, but differ on its cost: some stress lost Black officers, convention votes and offices. Older New Orleans players recall that Black musicians had no union or only short-lived ones, while later voices complain of weak union enforcement of scale.

communities.name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and collections tell stories about Lester Young, "Prez", mostly as he was in the 1920s through the 1950s. The community runs from his boyhood in the Young family band, through the territory bands (Bronson, the Blue Devils, Andy Kirk) and Kansas City jam sessions, to his years with Count Basie and his decline and death in 1959. Tellers agree that he was wholly original: a light, mellow tone, a way of improvising that avoided pet phrases, and a private slang and set of nicknames ("Lady Day", "Holy", "the slave") that also marked his personality. They often set him against Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster and Herschel Evans, and they disagree about how much he shaped the Basie sound and whether the supposed rivalry with Evans was real. The stories are told by sidemen who worked with him (Buddy Tate, Harry Edison, Jo Jones, Freddie Green), by early acquaintances from his youth and by younger players who met him late. Personal portraits dominate. They cover his gentleness and humor, his drinking, the mistreatment he met in the Henderson band, and his last days.

communities.name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection tell stories of practical jokes and horseplay among bandmates, mostly on the bandstand, the bus and the dressing room. Most are set between the 1920s and 1960s, in big bands (Ellington, Basie, Woody Herman, Tommy Dorsey, Whiteman) and in small groups such as the Oscar Peterson trio. The classic tricks recur across tellers: water poured in a tuba, soaped bows, stink bombs, limburger in a mouthpiece, swapped valves, firecrackers, hidden snare drums, alarm clocks on the bus. Bigard's Ellington stories from the 1920s and 30s, Woody Herman's Bill Harris and Chubby Jackson, and Buddy Rich, Joe Venuti and Spike Jones as notorious jokers keep returning. Tellers largely agree that humor kept a band together on the road, though Jacques Butler notes that teasing could drive thin-skinned players out. The cluster also draws in some neighboring mishap and "worst gig" stories (a clarinet falling apart mid-solo, an overloaded excursion boat, bad New Jersey gigs), and some loosely related items about musicians' personalities.

communities.name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days
communities.narrative: Across nearly a hundred interviews, mostly from Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive with Rutgers, Hamilton and Smithsonian voices, musicians are asked what tunes they and their bands actually played, and they answer by reeling off titles. The stories are set mainly between about 1900 and 1944, centred on New Orleans but also Chicago, St. Louis and touring shows. Tiger Rag recurs most often, with arguments over who played it first, what it was called before (Number Two, the CF and B-flat rag) and the words shouted in it, alongside Bugle Call Rag, High Society, Panama, blues, waltzes, quadrilles and polkas. Tellers agree that early bands played by ear, often with numbered rather than named tunes. They differ over whether the music came from ragtime books, Scott Joplin red-back rags, stock arrangements, pop songs or spirituals. Pianists, singers and trumpeters recall the repertoires of specific bands (Jack Carey, Celestin, Laine, Bolden, Wickliffe) and of their fathers. A few later accounts, from 1930s Chicago and 1950s-60s revival bands, describe building or shifting repertoire.

communities.name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, Chicago, New York and the touring South remember the women blues singers of the 1920s: Bessie Smith above all, then Mamie Smith, Ma Rainey, Clara Smith, Trixie Smith, Ethel Waters and Ida Cox. The stories are mostly set between about 1910 and 1930. Many tellers share a short list of favorites and rank the singers against each other. Billie Pierce and Herman Autrey rank them out loud: Pierce names Bessie and Ida Cox and dislikes Ma Rainey. Autrey places Ma below the louder, more dynamic Smiths, and Clara Smith above Mamie, who in his view never took with the public. A second strand is origins and business. Danny Barker, Garvin Bushell and Reb Spikes tell how Perry Bradford got Mamie Smith to record Crazy Blues in 1920, what she was like on stage, and the rush for singers named Smith that followed. A third strand is working with the singers: accompanying them on records and in theaters, the rival Smith shows, and touring blues shows. Louis Armstrong, Punch Miller and Herman Autrey tell these. Instrumentalists, bandleaders and fellow singers tell it differently from the few listeners such as Procope, who were unimpressed or never heard Bessie. Several tellers also draw the line between blues singers and popular or cabaret singers.

communities.name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection describe how they physically traveled while touring with bands, and what that life was like. The stories span roughly the 1920s to the 1960s, with later echoes from the 1970s to the 2000s. Earlier tellers recall Pullman cars, private berths, railroad-station sleeping and rented cars. Big-band veterans recall the Ellington and Calloway private railroad cars, the Basie bus, and sleeper buses. Later and smaller-group players describe station wagons, cramped overnight car rides and cheap hotels. The tellers agree that the road meant constant one-nighters, long overnight hauls, bad weather and breakdowns, such as blizzards, 28 below, and a bus losing its brakes. They also agree that it brought camaraderie and a first look at the country. They differ on whether it was a pleasure or a grind, and several compare the old road days with today's easier touring, or lament that young players no longer get the road apprenticeship. Band leaders such as Nat Towles, Ernie Fields and Don Albert appear as bus owners, bookers and employers, and a few segments drift into specific engagements or itineraries rather than the travel itself.

communities.name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, Texas, Chicago and New York talk about the plucked rhythm instruments: the banjo and the guitar, and the players who held them. The stories mostly run from about 1910 to 1960. Early on, guitars were universal in New Orleans bands until the banjo took over around 1915 for its drive. In the 1930s the banjo faded and the guitar came back as a rhythm instrument, sometimes held up near the microphone, as Theodore Bunn did with Ellington. Tellers argue over which instrument suits which music. Dixieland men such as Verrett and Pops Foster prefer the banjo, or the piano, to electric guitar. A second strand is amplification and the move to the Charlie Christian and T-Bone Walker era, with Eddie Durham's Seattle amp story and Clayton Duerr on microphones. The stories are told by rhythm players themselves (Danny Barker, the Marreros, Bunn, Verrett, Guesnon) and by sidemen and interviewers who remember the banjoists and guitarists in the bands they worked with. The strongest anchors are Charlie Christian and Freddie Green with Basie, along with New Orleans banjoists such as Johnny St. Cyr and the Marreros.

communities.name: Bandstand fights, knives and tempers
communities.narrative: Musicians tell stories of violent quarrels inside working bands, mostly set between the 1940s and the 1960s in New York and on the road. Two incidents anchor the cluster. The first is the 1941 Cab Calloway band episode, where a spitball led Cab to slap Dizzy Gillespie, Dizzy drew a knife, and he left the band. Danny Barker, Cozy Cole, Jonah Jones and Mario Bauza all tell it, and they differ on who threw the spitball and how bad the cut was. The second is Charles Mingus, whose temper runs through his sidemen's accounts: he punched Jimmy Knepper before the 1962 Town Hall concert, fought Jackie McLean in Cleveland, choked Tony Scott on a tour bus, tore up a piano over unpaid money, and clashed with Juan Tizol in Duke Ellington's band. The tellers are sidemen, often young players hired into these bands, and they tell the stories with a mix of fear, humour and affection. Smaller accounts of rivalries and feuds in other bands (Ben Webster's knife, Jacques Butler and Mavouzy, Ron Carter and Harold Mabern) show the same pattern. Some stories end in reconciliation and friendship, such as Cab and Dizzy years later, while others end with a firing.

communities.name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows
communities.narrative: This community gathers musicians' memories of the traveling and theatrical show business that employed many of them before and alongside jazz: minstrel shows, circus side-show bands, carnivals, medicine shows, tent shows, TOBA vaudeville circuits and, later, Broadway and revue stagework. Most stories are set between the 1910s and the 1940s. They run from the South and Midwest (North Carolina towns, Texas, Oklahoma, Illinois) to the theater circuits of New York, Chicago, Harlem and Washington. The tellers agree on the texture of the life: parades to draw crowds, Pullman cars or baggage cars as lodging, small weekly pay ($3 to $15), stranded troupes and managers who gambled away the money. They also agree that the road was where many learned to read, to play blues and to accompany dancers and comedians. They differ in scale and tone. Early-career players such as Freddie Moore, Eddie Durham, Herman Autrey and Eddie Barefield recount hardship and apprenticeship on tent and carnival shows. Performers such as Chuck Green, John W. Bubbles and Leonidas Young recall vaudeville acts, blackface routines and revues. A smaller group of later pit-band and Broadway musicians, such as Joe Wilder, compare theater shows with dance work. The cluster is large and loose at its edges, with some stray segments about individual theaters or interview mechanics.

communities.name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him
communities.narrative: This community gathers the many ways musicians talk about Bix Beiderbecke, the cornetist of the Wolverines, the Jean Goldkette band and the Paul Whiteman Orchestra, and his partner Frankie Trumbauer. The stories are set mostly in the 1920s, from Davenport, Chicago and New Orleans to New York, and run from first-hand encounters (sitting in beside him, hanging out with him, watching Whiteman's band at the St. Charles Theater) to second-hand knowledge gained from Gennett and Okeh records. Tellers broadly agree on his tone, taste and harmonic choices, and several credit him with changing their own playing, for example by convincing Wild Bill Davison to give up mutes. Opinions differ on the man and the myth: Artie Shaw and Jacques Butler remember a heavy drinker, Bud Freeman and Al Rose argue that the legend of his life has been misread, and Jimmy Maxwell and some Whiteman sidemen did not rate him. Another strand is the lineage around him, with Emmett Hardy as an alleged influence, Red Nichols and others as imitators, Trumbauer as an underrated partner, and later revivalists such as Warren Vaché and Vince Giordano. The tellers include New Orleans players, Chicagoans, Black and white swing-era musicians, arrangers such as Bill Challis, and later revivalists, so the community mixes eyewitnesses and admirers.

communities.name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands
communities.narrative: This community gathers the stories musicians tell about working for, with or around Frank Sinatra, mostly from the 1940s through the 1970s. Frank Sinatra is tagged in 44 of the 198 segments, and Las Vegas is the most common place, with the Sands, Caesars Palace and Cal-Neva Lodge at Lake Tahoe recurring. Two phases dominate. In the early one (1939-1948), Harry James and Tommy Dorsey sidemen remember him as a young band singer: his first night with James, his stage confidence, the Astor Roof, and his weak years around 1948. In the later one (1950s-70s), Red Norvo's quintet and sextet, John Collins, Harry Edison, Freddie Green, the Basie band and arrangers such as Johnny Mandel tell of lounge runs, tours to Australia, Reprise sessions, Nelson Riddle charts and the Caesars Palace incident. Tellers agree on his musicianship, his good ear, his perfectionism and his loyalty to jazz players. They differ on the details: Collins says the fight story was untrue, Pete Candoli mentions a gun incident, and Joe Turner felt snubbed. A smaller fringe covers other headliners with Vegas residencies (Peggy Lee, Dinah Shore, Petula Clark, Tony Bennett and Ella Fitzgerald). The tellers are mostly sidemen, accompanists and arrangers.

communities.name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie
communities.narrative: Musicians across many interviews, mostly from Hamilton's Fillius archive and tied to the Basie band, tell stories about the singer Joe Williams. The setting runs from the 1940s to the 1990s, centered on Chicago (Lionel Hampton's band at the Regal Theater, where Hampton says he hired Williams on the spot) and then on his years with Count Basie. Many remember hearing him with Basie at Birdland or Storyville, and credit his hit "Every Day" with reviving the big band in the early 1950s. Players who accompanied him, including Frank Foster, Henry Johnson, Derrick Gardner and Ed Shaughnessy on the Tonight Show, describe him as a kind, easy-to-work-with, swinging singer. They single out his blues, his ballads, his tenor-like timbre and his insistence on knowing a song's lyrics and story. Managers and biographers (Theodore Saunders, John Levy, Leslie Gourse) add the business side: hard times in the early 1950s, the 1962 split from Basie, and his own small groups. The tellers agree on the warmth and musicianship and differ mainly in how and when they first met him. Several segments mention Williams only in passing within other stories.

communities.name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her
communities.narrative: Nearly every segment in this community is a musician's recollection of Billie Holiday, set mostly between about 1930 and 1957 in New York, Chicago, Detroit, Boston and Washington. Tellers range from bandleaders and sidemen who worked beside her to people who only met her once. Count Basie, in a long interview that keeps steering back to her, talks about her year with his band in 1937-38, her loneliness, her habit of needling him on the job, and his denial that she was fired over refusing to sing the blues. Others place her in particular rooms: the Grand Terrace, Cafe Society, the Famous Door, the Uptown House and the 1958 Newport and Seven Ages of Jazz appearances. A recurring thread is her decline, with drugs, difficult men and managers, and late-life regret. John Simmons describes his violent relationship with her, and John Levy and Horace Henderson discuss her husband and her management. The tellers agree on her phrasing and her power as a stylist, but they disagree on who started her on drugs, whether she was fired, and how far Lady Sings the Blues can be trusted.

communities.name: Band singers and accompanying vocalists
communities.narrative: Instrumentalists across eras talk about the singers they worked beside: the vocalists who fronted or sat with big bands, and the craft of accompanying them. The big-band stories are set mostly in the 1930s and 40s, with Ivie Anderson with Ellington, the Erskine Hawkins vocalists, Harry James, Les Brown, Basie and Billie Holiday, and Sinatra coming up through Tommy Dorsey. In these, tellers recall who sang, how they looked and behaved, and how the band felt about them. Abe Most says players resented vocalists because singing cost them solo choruses. Harry Edison says singers once just sat on the bandstand, and Frank Foster says the band loved Sinatra, Eckstine, Vaughan and Bennett for their jazz mentality. A second strand, told by pianists, bassists and drummers from the 1950s to the 2000s, is the art of accompanying: knowing the changes and keys, listening, and supporting the singer, as with Sarah Vaughan, Betty Carter, Carmen McRae, Ella Fitzgerald, Anita O'Day and Nina Simone. A third strand is personal portraits of individual singers, above all Sarah Vaughan, from John Malachi's tomboy stories to Horn Shirley's recollections. The tellers disagree about whether singers were an ornament to the band or a musical equal.

communities.name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection talk about what it takes to lead a band, and about what it was like to work under leaders. The stories run from the 1920s and 30s big bands (Sam Wooding, Ernie Fields, Jimmie Lunceford, Barnet) through the Basie, Ellington, Herman, Buddy Rich and Thad Jones/Mel Lewis orchestras to today's small-group leaders such as Orrin Evans, Joanne Brackeen and Mark Soskin. Leaders describe the practical work: choosing sidemen for reliability, chemistry and humility, paying people fairly, booking gigs, dealing with promoters, firing players and keeping a steady group together. Sidemen describe what they learned from leaders, including Blakey's bandstand lessons and Thad Jones's writing, and what they put up with, such as Buddy Rich's temper. The tellers largely agree that a band is a collective effort, that a leader needs fairness, discipline and a good ear for people, and that long-running bands build a sound. They differ on style and structure: democratic equal-share bands against a single artistic leader, and artistic leaders against business leaders in co-led groups. Some musicians, like Bud Freeman, say leading was a mistake.

communities.name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people
communities.narrative: Musicians from every generation of the Basie orchestra, and from outside it, tell stories about Count Basie's band and what it was like to hear it, join it or sit in its chairs. The settings run from the Kansas City days of Bennie Moten, the Reno Club and Pop Monroe's, through the 1936 Savoy arrival and the Old Testament band, to the 1950s Birdland years and the 1970s-90s bands after Basie's death. Tellers agree that the band's greatness lay in a relaxed, spare feel built on the rhythm section: Freddie Green's guitar pulse, Walter Page and Jo Jones in the early days, Sonny Payne later. They also agree that Basie led almost without words, using a look, a gesture or a single finger, with Marshall Royal as straw boss. They differ on which band was best, the 1938 head-arrangement band or the 1950s-60s arranger-built band. Alumni such as Snooky Young, Clark Terry, Buddy Tate, Frank Foster and Butch Miles tell insider stories, while players who turned down or only briefly visited the band, and critics and radio hosts, tell the outsider version. Recruitment and job offers recur: Basie telegraphing Arnett Cobb, hearing Jimmy Lewis, and Terry or Wess recommending players.

communities.name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives talk about who handled the business side of their careers: personal managers, booking agents, agencies and business managers. The stories run from the 1920s road bands through the swing-era agencies (William Morris, MCA, GAC, Moe Gale's office, Joe Glaser's Associated Booking) to the 1990s and early 2000s, with most set in New York and other big-city hubs. Tellers describe how they found or lost a manager, what the agencies took (fifty percent of a band, five percent commissions, 25 percent management contracts), and how contracts were bought out or sold on. Some, like Kid Thomas Valentine, Sam Wooding and Lanny Morgan, managed and booked themselves, while Horn Shirley worked with John Levy on a handshake. Opinions split sharply. Joe Glaser and John Levy are praised for honesty and straight answers, while other bookers are called crooked, exploitative or merely lukewarm. Bandleaders, singers, sidemen and a few non-musicians such as managers and engineers tell these stories. They are mostly practical accounts of commissions, trust and control rather than musical ones.

communities.name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands
communities.narrative: Musicians from all four archives tell stories about jazz on the air: radio stations, network staff jobs and, above all, television. The earliest accounts are 1920s-30s radio, such as Kid Ory's band broadcasting on KFI in 1921, Bill Challis arranging at a fast pace for Paul Whiteman-era radio, and remote broadcasts that built bands and made clubs like Birdland known nationally. The 1940s-50s stories centre on getting into the CBS, NBC and ABC staffs. Eddie Barefield became the first Black staff musician at the Blue Network, Milt Hinton got into CBS through Jack Lesberg, and Al Hall describes being stonewalled in CBS interviews amid quota politics. From the 1950s on, the stories move to television: live variety shows (Your Show of Shows, Andy Williams, Steve Allen, Ed Sullivan, Arthur Godfrey), Billy Taylor's educational jazz series, and the long-running band chairs on The Tonight Show and later Saturday Night Live. Tellers disagree less about facts than about what the work meant. Some treat it as steady, well-paid, schedule-friendly employment that left evenings free for other bands, while others stress the hustle of auditions and the barriers of race. The tellers include sidemen and arrangers, bandleaders and singers, and also critics, producers and engineers who made or covered the broadcasts, mostly in New York and Los Angeles.

communities.name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition
communities.narrative: Musicians tell how brass players made horns talk with mutes, both bought and improvised. The setting is mostly 1910s to 1950s New Orleans, Chicago and Harlem. The earliest tellers (Joseph Rene, Ed Garland, Jack Kelly, Albert Walters) recall Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit, King Oliver and Freddie Keppard using plungers, derby hats, coconut shells, glasses, tin cans and eggshells. The story then moves to New York, where Johnny Dunn, Bubber Miley and Tricky Sam Nanton developed the growl and wa-wa sound in Duke Ellington's band, and Cootie Williams and Clark Terry learned the craft from that line. Players such as Herman Autrey and Vic Dickenson describe learning the Harmon, buzz and plunger mutes from specific teachers and swapping them. Where they differ is on credit and origins: Autrey claims the muted style before Jonah Jones, Terry denies owing his half-valve playing to Rex Stewart, and the manufacturers who sold the ideas back to players come up as a grievance. A smaller strand covers mutes in arranging and recording, such as Basie keeping Buck Clayton in a cup mute on records, and Ed Polcer and Joe Wilder demonstrating mute types.

communities.name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: This community collects the stories musicians tell about their first paying work: the first gig, the first band that hired them, and what it paid. The sums are small and remembered precisely: $2 for four hours in 1903, fifty cents a night plus tips at a 1930s Louisiana nightclub, $3 in a Rock Island trio, $25 for bongos at a wedding, $70 from a high school band director. Most tellers started as teenagers, often 12 to 16. Many were brought in by a father, mother, teacher or older player, and some were underpaid or not paid at all until a parent stepped in. The settings run from New Orleans social clubs, Pensacola fraternal halls and Prohibition-era bootleg dance places to Harlem theatres, roadhouses and, later, high school top-40 bands and weddings. Most stories are set between about 1916 and 1960, but a tail of younger players recalls the 1970s to 1990s. Older players tell of pickup jobs with local leaders such as Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit and Earl Hood, while younger ones describe school bands and family encouragement. Across the eras the tellers agree that the first job was about experience more than money, and they differ mainly in the era's wages and venues.

communities.name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music
communities.narrative: Across New Orleans, New York, Chicago and Los Angeles, musicians describe the non-music work that paid the bills alongside, or in place of, playing. The core stories are set from the 1910s through the 1950s: coal wagons, longshore and cotton-mill work, blacksmithing, barbering, cement finishing, shipyard welding, hospital and bank jobs, and the pressing shop or furniture store. Older New Orleans players such as Foster, LaCaze, Loyacano and Shields treat a day job as the normal condition of the trade, with most men playing nights after a full shift. Others describe leaving music when work dried up or pay was too low, then returning later, as Eddie Dawson, Clarence Ford and Willie Foster do. Later and more professional players frame the job differently. Melba Liston, Ruth Brisbane, Mike Wofford and Cosimo Matassa took a steady job for security, to leave time to practice, or to cover a gap, and several of them describe it as temporary or as something they resented. The tellers agree that music alone rarely supported a household. They differ on whether the day job was a sideline, a rescue, or a late-career pension.

communities.name: The Depression years and the WPA band
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the early 1930s, when the Depression cut work, pay and the whole music business, and many New Orleans players ended up in the government-sponsored ERA and WPA bands. The WPA band (about 119 to 135 players at its largest, later shrinking) rehearsed daily, often at the Fifth Ward Club on Dumaine Street, under directors such as Louis Dumaine. It paid a steady monthly wage of roughly nineteen dollars a week, played concerts in parks, schools and hospitals, and appeared at events like a Roosevelt visit, but it never played dances. Tellers disagree on whether it was a lifeline or a trap. Some joined for three years or more, some were kept out by politics or by reading tests, and some quit or skipped it for small pick-up bands. Those small bands paid pennies, such as a dollar or six bits a night on Decatur Street, in contrast to the few who say they always had work, like Ellington's band or Armstrong. Most tellers are New Orleans players interviewed at Tulane, with Chicago and New York musicians adding their own accounts of lean years, radio work and cheap food.

communities.name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom
communities.narrative: Musicians from all four archives weigh the big band against the small group, and talk about the rehearsal work that held big bands together. The main story is a trade-off. Big bands meant written arrangements, section discipline and solo space handed out by the leader or arranger. Small groups, sitting in and jam sessions meant freedom to play as long as you liked. Vic Dickenson, Benny Waters, Big Nick Nicholas, Omer Simeon, Barney Bigard, Maxine Sullivan, Annie Ross, Carmen Leggio and Richard Wyands all say, in nearly the same words, that they preferred small settings. Bigard, for example, compares Armstrong's small band with Ellington's cliques and eight-bar solos. The second strand is how bands actually rehearsed. Don Albert's band rehearsed almost daily on the road and kept 150 or more numbered arrangements straight. Charlie Barnet and Quentin Jackson recall Don Redman's rehearsal methods. Others describe sloppy or boring rehearsals, and bandleaders such as Horace Silver, Roscoe Mitchell and Jon Hendricks have their own rehearsal habits. Most stories are set from the 1930s to the 1990s. Sidemen of the swing era tell the big-band side, and modern players and leaders tell the rehearsal and format-preference side. Some, like Bill Watrous and Vince Lateano, defend the big band.

communities.name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used
communities.narrative: Drummers, mostly from New Orleans but also from New York, Chicago and the swing bands, describe the physical equipment of their instrument and how it changed. The oldest stories are set in the 1900s to 1920s. They recall rope-tension and single-head gut-snare drums, big 26 to 28 inch bass drums with overhanging or homemade pedals, Chinese cymbals, cowbells, wood blocks, tom-toms and the slapstick. Many of them tell of their first set, or of a father's or older player's kit. Later tellers move into the 1930s and after: the hi-hat, wire brushes, Zildjian and Paiste cymbals, and brand choices among Leedy, Ludwig and Gretsch. Louie Bellson's invention of the double-bass-drum kit and Ray Bauduc's custom splash cymbal belong here. The tellers agree that early kits were improvised and piecemeal and that equipment shrank and standardized over time. They differ on who first used particular items, such as the washboard, the folding bass drum and the slapstick. Interviewers such as William Russell and Allen prompt many of the accounts, which often name drummers like Baby Dodds, Zutty Singleton and Jo Jones as models. Almost all the tellers are drummers, with a few other New Orleans players describing the drummers they heard.

communities.name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: This community gathers musicians' memories of the Savoy Ballroom in Harlem, the home ground of Chick Webb's orchestra, and of the battles of the bands that made it famous. The stories run mostly from the Savoy's opening in 1926 through the late 1930s and into 1941. Early tellers such as Charlie Holmes, Happy Caldwell and Teddy McRae recall the house bands (Fess Williams, the Savoy Bearcats, Webb) and their first awed nights on the floor. Later tellers such as Count Basie, Mario Bauza, Lionel Hampton and Jay McShann describe set-piece contests against Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, Benny Goodman, Lucky Millinder and the Savoy Sultans. Visiting bands tell it as a test, whether it was Basie's no-battle courtesy, McShann's Kansas City band holding back and then outplaying Millinder, or Gus Johnson's story of arriving late and being called Western Dogs. The tellers disagree mainly on who won, and each tells it from their own band's side. A smaller group of stories moves away from the Savoy to contests elsewhere (Detroit's Graystone, Kansas City, Chicago), and a few mention the Savoy only in passing.

communities.name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong
communities.narrative: This is the broad, many-voiced Louis Armstrong story, told by 281 interviewees across Tulane, Rutgers, Hamilton and the Smithsonian. Its anchor is Armstrong himself, whom nearly every segment tags. The period runs from his New Orleans boyhood (the Colored Waifs' Home, the Tuxedo brass band, Fate Marable's riverboat band, c. 1913-19) through Chicago and New York in the 1920s-30s (King Oliver, Erskine Tate's pit at the Vendome, the Rhythm Club, Luis Russell, Fletcher Henderson) to the All Stars and world tours of the 1940s-60s. Sidemen such as Trummy Young, Cozy Cole, Teddy McRae and Zutty Singleton describe working in his bands: the personnel, the rehearsals, the Goodman-Armstrong tour, and life on the road with his generosity, humor and Swiss Kriss. A strong sub-story is manager Joe Glaser, with his handshake deal, his handling of Louis's money and how he came to manage him. Others, from Doc Cheatham and Sweets Edison to Ira Gitler, tell what hearing or replacing Armstrong meant, treating him as an idol and as the first great soloist. The tellers agree on his warmth, his stature and his influence. They differ in vantage point: boyhood witnesses, bandmates, rival trumpeters, and later critics and family friends.

communities.name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique
communities.narrative: Musicians across many interviews talk about the string bass and the players who defined it. The stories are set mostly between the 1910s and the 1960s, in New Orleans, New York, Chicago, St. Louis and on the road with big bands, above all Ellington's. New Orleans players such as Pops Foster, Wellman Braud, Steve Brown, Kimball and Jimmy Johnson are remembered as the first bassists, and the tellers compare them on ear, tone, reading and bowing. The tellers then trace a lineage through Jimmy Blanton, Slam Stewart, Oscar Pettiford, Milt Hinton, Ray Brown, Paul Chambers and Ron Carter, with Mingus and Walter Booker explaining why Blanton changed the instrument. Other strands are craft and equipment: bowing, taped fingers against blisters, aluminum and plywood basses, and the arrival of amplification, the Fender bass and the electric bass, which several bassists say pushed the upright out of studio work. Bassists tell most of these stories themselves, while drummers, horn players and pianists add portraits and opinions about who was best. A minority of segments only mention a bassist in passing, as a name to be identified or a friend, so the cluster is centered on the instrument more than on one event.

communities.name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Across more than 500 interviews, musicians talk about drummers: who the great ones were, who they heard as boys, who they worked beside, and what separated a good drummer from a merely loud one. The New Orleans tellers (Tulane) list the early generation, such as Red Happy, John Vigne, Henry Zeno, Black Benny, Zutty Singleton and Baby Dodds, usually in short ranked roll calls set in the 1900s to 1930s. Swing and bebop players talk about Sid Catlett, Chick Webb, Jo Jones, Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich, Kenny Clarke, Max Roach and later Elvin Jones, praising Catlett's melodic, gentle playing and Jones's lift. A second strand moves from naming drummers to analyzing the craft: time-keeping and the afterbeat, supporting the band versus showmanship and solos, and playing written parts in reading bands. Big-band sidemen and bandleaders tend to judge drummers by how they drove the section. Younger players such as Jackie McLean, Curtis Fuller and Kenny Barron extend the list into the 1960s and later, with Roy Haynes, Roy Brooks and Freddie Waits. The tellers largely agree on Catlett and Webb as benchmarks, and differ on whether flash or restraint made the better drummer.

communities.name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans and well beyond recall what people actually danced to, and what the band had to play for them. The stories run from the 1870s Creole kalenda and bamboula, through the quadrilles, mazurkas, schottisches, polkas and lancers of the 1890s-1910s, to the one-step, two-step, slow drag, turkey trot, shimmy and Charleston, and on to swing-era dance bands and 1950s-60s fads like the Bunny Hop. Tellers such as Alice Zeno, Ray Lopez, Milton "Mooney" Martin and Louis James describe how the figures were called and in what order a dance night ran, including the waltz every few sets and the quadrille coming on around eleven. Territory-band and later dance-band players (Buster Smith, Eddie Johnson, Luke Schiro, Jim Robinson) focus on repertoire, set length, stock waltzes and playing sweet or danceable music. Tellers differ on whether jazz bands played the older dances at all: Alex Bigard says only the orchestras played quadrilles, while others say their bands played waltzes and ragtime for them. A late strand, voiced by Houston Person and Marian McPartland, laments or remembers jazz losing its tie to dancing.

communities.name: Listening to classical music, then and now
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives talk about what they themselves listen to away from the bandstand, and for a large share of them the answer is classical music. Stravinsky, Bartok, Ravel, Prokofiev, Shostakovich, Beethoven, Mozart and Chopin recur as favorites, with Rachmaninoff, Elgar and Debussy appearing less often. Tellers such as JJ Johnson, Mose Allison, Hubert Laws and George Avakian recall a particular moment of discovery: hearing The Rite of Spring at Johnny Carisi's home, modern classical listening at LSU, or Stravinsky in Boston. Many give a current-listening inventory, sometimes mixed with older big bands, Brazilian music or opera, and sometimes with remarks on CDs and headphones or a habit of not playing their own records. Earlier-generation stories (Bix and the Wolverines at the symphony, Armstrong's open ears, Ellington's band admired by classical players) show the same curiosity set in the 1920s. The tellers agree that classical music fed their writing and ears, but they differ in taste. Laws prefers the Russians and is cool toward Mozart and Bartok, while Mingus came to Beethoven late and Allison and Johnson treat Bartok as a source. Mostly pianists, flutists, arrangers and horn players tell it, and it runs from the 1920s through the 1990s.

communities.name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: This community gathers New Orleans musicians' memories of playing and watching street parades, above all Mardi Gras and the parades of social and pleasure clubs, benevolent societies and brass bands. Most stories are set between about 1900 and 1960, mainly in the city's streets (Canal Street, Claiborne, St. Charles, Algiers). Tellers describe the practical side of the job: marching for hours in the heat, walking on shells and rocks, alternating two bands so players could rest, and the low pay (one man recalls 35 cents for an all-day march). They also remember the pageantry: Rex and Zulu arriving by boat, flambeaux torch carriers, a Lions Club parade with a live lion, the Bulls Club night parade, umbrellas, uniforms and the rough second line. Older players such as Barbarin, Laine, Bigard and Don Albert recall the early brass bands (Eureka, Tuxedo, Chris Kelly's) and their rivalries, while later players such as Bob Watts and John E. Wood compare the 1950s and 1960s with how parades look in the 1980s. A few tellers set the same traditions elsewhere (Mobile, Pass Christian, Thibodaux, Chicago, Berlin). Nearly all the tellers are in the Tulane collection, and they are mostly brass-band and dance-band players.

communities.name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line
communities.narrative: This community gathers New Orleans musicians' accounts of playing for and watching funerals, mostly Black benevolent-society and brass-band funerals, with a few white-band and out-of-town variants. The stories range from the 1890s through the 1950s and 60s, with a small number of later reflections, and are set chiefly in New Orleans, especially Algiers and Gretna. Tellers agree on the core pattern: slow hymns and dirges on the way to the grave, then livelier "hot" music and a second line on the return. They also recall wakes, society halls where processions assembled, and the uniforms, umbrellas and horse-drawn hearses of the old days. They differ on change over time: some say funerals are now cautious about offending families, run at any hour, or draw tourists and white onlookers, while others stress that musicians still play them for fun and for the pay. Veterans such as Danny Barker, Joseph Rene, Papa Jack Laine and Red Clark tell which bands (Eureka, Tuxedo, Chris Kelly's) worked funerals and how jobs were won. Younger revivalists, collectors and outsiders add observations on the custom and its spread.

communities.name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Musicians recall joining, playing in and leaving Lionel Hampton's orchestra, mostly from his first big band in 1940 through the late 1940s and early 1950s. Early tellers such as Marshall Royal, Charles Thompson and Quentin Jackson describe how the band was assembled in Los Angeles around the Les Hite alumni, with Nat King Cole recommending Thompson and Illinois Jacquet in the saxophone section. Later sidemen, including Joe Wilder, Arnett Cobb, Teddy McRae, Zeke Mullins and Art Farmer, tell how they were hired, often by phone call or a rehearsal audition, and who sat beside them. Hampton himself appears as a gifted, boyish showman on drums, vibes and piano. Several tellers also describe him as a demanding bandleader who underpaid players, kept record contracts to himself and left sidemen to pay for dinners. The stories connect to adjacent big-band jobs, with Lunceford and Hite the most common, because players often moved between these bands. Beyond the core group, a few loosely related segments (other Hamptons, Hampton Hawes, Slide Hampton) were pulled in by name similarity.

communities.name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope
communities.narrative: This community collects the many small stories musicians tell about what they were actually paid, and how that pay was set, shared, shorted or skimmed. The tellers quote weekly salaries and nightly rates with unusual precision: six dollars a night in country dance bands of the 1900s-1910s, $50-100 a week in the 1919 Syncopated Orchestra, $60-110 in Harlem and Roseland bands around 1929-33, $90 with Woody Herman in the 1940s-50s, and $550-1300 for trios and single acts in the 1950s. Around the figures sit recurring mechanics: union scale versus what leaders really paid, tips and the kitty split with the leader, percentage jobs and door takes, kickbacks, being docked to cover a predecessor's debt, and managers or booking agents like Joe Glaser or MCA. The setting runs mostly from the 1910s to about 1960, centered on New York, Chicago and New Orleans, with later voices (arrangers, producers, club players of the 1970s-2000s) describing fees, royalties and working for exposure. Tellers largely agree that pay on the road and with famous leaders was poor, and that steady theater, hotel or club work paid better. They differ in tone, from rueful resentment to pride in making good money or simply playing for love.

communities.name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Across 302 interviews from all four archives, musicians tell the story of leaving a band: giving notice, being fired, or watching the group fold. It is set mostly between the 1930s and 1970s, with later examples from Miles Davis, Lookout Farm and the Dave Liebman groups. The reasons are strikingly consistent. Tellers cite exhaustion with the road and one-nighters, low or unpaid wages, stale repertoire, cliques and quarrels, the showmanship of JATP, a wife's wishes, and the wish to lead their own group or study, write or move to a better-paying job. Big-band men (Ellington, Calloway, Hampton, Dorsey, Moten, Eckstine) describe leaving the leader's orchestra, while younger bop and post-bop players describe leaving Dizzy, Blakey, Miles, Cannonball or Tatum. They differ in tone: some leave on warm terms with the leader reluctantly letting them go, others quit angrily, and a few tell of leaders who disbanded for lack of money or a bad booker. Sidemen and leaders both tell it, from different sides of the stand.

communities.name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how
communities.narrative: This community gathers the many moments when interviewers ask a musician about trombone players and the musician names who he admired, played beside or thought overrated. The largest share is New Orleans: Tulane interviewees from the 1900s to the 1920s run through Zue Robertson, Frankie Duson, Harrison Bradley, Roy Palmer, Jim Robinson, Earl Humphrey, Morris French and others. They compare tone, speed, reading versus faking, and parade men versus dance-hall men. A second strand comes from swing and bebop players, who talk about Jack Teagarden, Lawrence Brown, Dickie Wells, Tricky Sam Nanton and Trummy Young. A third strand covers J.J. Johnson, Curtis Fuller and Slide Hampton, and younger players on trombone sound, technique and legacy, including the trombone choirs and Hip-Bone Music. The tellers agree that individual trombonists had distinct, recognizable styles. They differ on who counts as the best, and some are openly sceptical, as when Higginbotham's son says Teagarden was overrated or Danny Barker says Jim Robinson is overrated by the revivalists. Most stories are told in answer to a direct prompt like "who were your favorite trombonists?", so many segments are short lists of names with a line of judgment.

communities.name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road
communities.narrative: This community gathers musicians' accounts of drugs and drinking in jazz life, set mostly between the 1920s and 1960 in New York, Chicago, New Orleans, Kansas City and Los Angeles. The earliest tellers recall whiskey, wine, reefer ("muggles" and "tea"), opium and cocaine. Many then describe heroin arriving in the bebop era of the 1940s and 50s, often linked to Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, Miles Davis and later Chet Baker and Art Pepper. Explanations for the shift differ: wartime stress, loose freedom, young players without grounding, the pressure and itinerancy of the road, easy access, or frustration with a society that held jazz in contempt. Many speakers stress their own abstinence ("stayed a Boy Scout", stuck to whiskey), and others tell of a first marijuana experience, a heroin arrest that cost a cabaret card, or a bandmate who quit drinking through AA. Interviewers often ask about it directly, and some musicians decline to name names or argue that heroin was a plague on the business rather than typical of jazz.

communities.name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: This community gathers stories about bodies failing and lives ending: strokes, surgeries, hearing loss, accidents, and the deaths of colleagues and bandleaders. The tellers span the whole century, from 1920s New Orleans bandsmen like Little Dad and Buddy Petit to 1990s and 2000s accounts of Melba Liston's stroke, Elvin Jones's bypass and Art Taylor-era grief over Dizzy Gillespie, Tito Puente and Billy Higgins. Many are first-person health episodes: Bell's palsy, pneumonia that cost a first show, tinnitus, a ruined hand or lost sight, and what it did to playing and to a career. Others are elegiac, with a musician recalling how he heard of a friend's death, the funeral, or a last recording and a last gig. Sidemen and singers tell it as much as famous leaders, and the stories run across all four archives, with New York the commonest setting. They agree that illness interrupts playing and that musicians mourn each other closely; they differ in tone, from clinical recovery narratives to grief and, occasionally, blunt accounts of drinking or smoking behind an early death.

communities.name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: This community gathers hundreds of short recollections in which musicians, overwhelmingly in the Hogan Jazz Archive interviews, name and describe the places where dance bands worked in New Orleans, mostly between about 1900 and the 1940s. The core is the society and benevolent-association halls (Economy Hall, Francs Amis, Hope's Hall, Artesian, Globe, Perseverance, Cooperators), along with the Plum Plan hall, the uptown and downtown halls, and across-the-river spots in Algiers and Gretna. Around that sit the lakefront resorts and camps at Milneburg and West End, and parks and pleasure grounds such as Johnson Park, Lincoln Park and Beville Park, where bands played Sunday picnics. Tellers mostly list halls they played or frequented, compare them for acoustics or ease of playing, and place them in the social order of the city (who played for which club or social level). They also touch on admission prices, pay, and the later fate of the buildings, many of which became churches. A smaller fringe moves outside New Orleans to ballrooms and dance halls in New York, Columbus, Chicago and Mobile, and a few segments are interview mechanics such as reel changes. The stories are told by veteran New Orleans players of every generation, by researchers like Bill Russell who prompt them, and by a few outsiders.

communities.name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable
communities.narrative: This community gathers New Orleans, St. Louis and visiting musicians' memories of the Streckfus Line excursion steamers (the Capitol, St. Paul, Sidney, J.S., Island Queen) and above all Fate Marable's band, which held the boats from roughly 1919 into the 1930s. Tellers describe how they were hired, often by recommendation or after a New Orleans player was sent for from St. Louis, and what the job demanded: stock arrangements, a strict reading band, weekly rehearsals, a captain who timed the numbers, and piano players who had to play the calliope. Others recall the boat from the dock or the levee as listeners: the calliope announcing the steamer, Monday-night dances for Black patrons, and the way the Streckfus brothers split the society crowd and the ordinary crowd between boats. Rival bands (Charlie Creath, Dewey Jackson, Sidney Desvigne, Piron) and band personnel come up repeatedly, along with Louis Armstrong's and Pops Foster's time aboard. The accounts mostly agree on Marable's discipline and prestige; they differ in whether the boats were a sustained job, a single night, or a formative apprenticeship. Most tellers are New Orleans-born Black musicians interviewed by Tulane and Rutgers, with a few later St. Louis players like Clark Terry.

communities.name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring
communities.narrative: This community gathers stories of jazz musicians who worked in movies, television and the studios, mostly in Hollywood and Los Angeles but also New York and Paris. The period runs from silent films of the late 1920s through the 1930s-40s feature films and shorts (Cabin in the Sky, A Song Is Born, Jammin' the Blues, New Orleans, Crossfire) to 1950s-70s scoring and TV work and a few much later credits such as The Terminal and Northern Exposure. Tellers fall into two groups. Performers recall appearing or playing on camera, miming solos to a prerecorded track, getting small or unused parts, and sometimes being asked to remember cast and personnel, often prompted by an interviewer's film credits. Composers, arrangers and studio players such as Benny Golson, Johnny Mandel, Gerald Wilson and Red Callender describe the craft of scoring to picture, orchestrators, deadlines and the studio contractors. They differ in tone: Callender says "jazz" was a dirty word to film contractors, while Mingus complains that black musicians were shut out of film and TV and others call the studio work a good living beside jazz.

communities.name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four collections tell how they, their friends or their bands acquired a name. The stories run from the 1900s to the 1950s, with a few later ones, and are set in New Orleans, New York, Chicago and Kansas City. In most of them a nickname is given by chance, often by someone else: a hat (Panama), a football tackle (Cozy), a riverboat habit of fidgeting (Wiggles), a girl calling out in Philadelphia (Hymie), a bandleader garbling a name (Red Norvo). The same logic applies to bands and venues. The Eureka band, Kid Thomas's band, the Shawees, the Spirits of Rhythm, Machito and his Afro-Cubans and the Palladium's Blen Blen club were each named after a person, a tune or a club owner's decision. Tellers mostly agree that the name arrived by accident and then stuck on records, posters or in the press. Some differ in tone: Count Basie declines to explain "Count", while Armstrong and Pops Foster give detailed origin stories. The cluster also picks up neighbouring talk about band slang, musicians' jargon, and how to spell or pronounce a name.

communities.name: Going west: moving to and working in California
communities.narrative: Musicians from all four archives tell about the pull of California, above all Los Angeles and secondarily San Francisco, and about what working there was like. The earliest stories, set in the late 1920s through the 1940s, are by Black players on Central Avenue and in the big clubs: Lawrence Brown with Curtis Mosby at the Apex Club and the Cotton Club, Marshall Royal on movie stars at Sebastian's, and Teddy Edwards and JJ Johnson on Billy Berg's and the bebop arrivals of 1945. Many other tellers recount the decision to move west, whether in 1940 on a freighter to San Pedro, after a marriage ended, for an NBC staff job, or when the Tonight Show relocated to Hollywood. Later musicians from the 1960s through the 2000s describe the trade-offs of living there: space, weather, studio work and television money against leaving New York, with some deciding to stay and others, like Wild Bill Davison and Chazz Frichtel, leaving again or planning to. The tellers broadly agree that California offered openness and steady work, but they differ on whether it suited jazz, since several chose the Bay Area or San Diego over smoggy Los Angeles and some regretted the studio life.

communities.name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues
communities.narrative: Musicians recall their first encounters with the blues and try to say what the form is and where it came from. Most stories are set between about 1900 and the 1950s, centred on Memphis, New Orleans, Texas, Mississippi and Chicago. Many are tied to W. C. Handy, with tellers such as Jasper Taylor, Jeff Riddick, Lovie Austin and J. C. Higginbotham describing Memphis Blues and St. Louis Blues, his syndicate, his royalties and his only record. Others place the blues in New Orleans with Buddy Bolden and the Robichaux and Eureka bands, or in Texas with Blind Lemon Jefferson, Lead Belly and Texas Alexander. Tellers disagree on origins: railroad workers and the plantation, feeling inherited from slavery, a Southern language, or something not indigenous to New Orleans, as Al Rose argues. Later musicians such as Harold Mabern, Branford Marsalis, Clay Jenkins and Bob Cranshaw describe studying the blues as the anchor of jazz. Most tellers are New Orleans and swing-era players interviewed by Tulane and Rutgers, with a few modern players looking back.

communities.name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene
communities.narrative: This is the Chicago story as told by hundreds of musicians, most of them New Orleans players and their Black Chicago contemporaries, set mainly between about 1916 and 1946. Tellers recall the journey north, often tied to a particular bandleader (Manuel Perez, Freddie Keppard, King Oliver, the Original Dixieland Jazz Band) or to a date they try to pin down, such as when Tubby Hall went in 1917. They then list the places and jobs: the State Street and 35th Street South Side, Dreamland, Royal Gardens, the Deluxe, Pekin, Sunset Cafe, Plantation, Grand Terrace and Club DeLisa. Alongside the venues they name the bands and sidemen they worked with, including Jimmie Noone, Earl Hines, Erskine Tate, Stuff Smith and Fletcher Henderson. Many segments are interviewers (William Russell, Danny Barker and others) sorting out who played where and when, so the tone is part reminiscence and part reconstructing a map and a roster. Later tellers, such as bebop-era and 1950s-60s players, extend the scene into the swing years, the Blue Note and Jazz Showcase, but the core remains the 1910s-30s migration and the cabaret circuit. Tellers agree on Chicago as the magnet and on Oliver's and Noone's bands as its benchmarks, and differ mostly on dates, personnel and club locations.

communities.name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: This is the roll-call story: asked about a band, the musician lists who was in it. Interviewers press for names, instruments and section make-up, and tellers reconstruct lineups from memory, from photographs and scrapbooks, or from old newspaper notices. The stories are set mostly between about 1910 and 1950. New Orleans bands dominate (Sam Morgan, Jack Carey, Kid Rena, Sidney Desvigne, Peter Bocage, the Eureka and Tuxedo brass bands), but Chicago, New York, Kansas City and territory big bands (Moten, Redman, Luis Russell, Basie, Ellington alumni) appear too, along with a few later or non-US groups such as Ken Colyer's Crane River band and Carla Bley's ensembles. Tellers agree that a band is defined by its members and often settle on size, such as six pieces against twelve, or the union counting a drummer as two. They differ in how sure they are. Some give confident lists, while others say they cannot recall the trombonist or drummer, or the interviewers sort out which Johnson is meant. Tulane and Rutgers interviews supply most of the segments, and the tellers are sidemen and leaders alike.

communities.name: Fiddlers and reading violinists of New Orleans
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about the violin players they knew or heard, mostly in New Orleans from the 1890s to the 1920s. Interviewees, drawn largely from the Tulane archive, name and rank the downtown Creole violinists (Peter Bocage, Armand Piron, Paul Dominguez, John Robichaux, Manuel Manetta, Herbert Lindsay, Max Fink) and others such as Oscar Marco and Valto. Violin often led the early string and dance bands, and the players were prized as sight-readers and bandleaders who were sometimes seen as bossy businessmen. Tellers differ on whether the jazz fiddlers of the 1910s and 20s matched the older, stricter "professor" violinists. A smaller strand moves outside New Orleans to the jazz violin of Joe Venuti, Stuff Smith, Eddie South and Stephane Grappelli. These stories come from Rutgers, Hamilton and Smithsonian interviews with swing-era and later musicians and musicians' peers.

communities.name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation
communities.narrative: Musicians, mostly New Orleans veterans interviewed for the Hogan Jazz Archive, are asked to reconstruct how the early bands were put together: how many men, which instruments, and who played them. The stories are set between the 1890s and the early 1930s. They start with the boys' bands and country brass bands of 10 to 18 men, move to the six- or seven-piece string bands and small dance combinations, and end with the larger show, society and big bands of the 1920s and 30s. Tellers broadly agree that the older string bands used guitar, bass, violin and mandolin with no piano. Brass and dance bands settled on cornet or trumpet, clarinet, trombone, bass and drums, with banjo and saxophone coming in later and piano arriving last. They differ on details such as whether violins dropped out before the war, whether guitars could be heard against brass, and what counts as a real jazz band. Much of the material is interviewer-driven roll-call, with the musician naming members of a named band (Magnolia, Superior, Sam Morgan's, Eagle, Raceland) and assigning each an instrument. Some tellers are older Black Creole players, some are white players from Papa Jack Laine's circle, and a few are later bandleaders and sidemen.

communities.name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists
communities.narrative: This community gathers musicians' portraits of the great jazz saxophonists, with Coleman Hawkins at the center of nearly every story. The tellers, from Hamilton, Rutgers, Tulane and Smithsonian interviews, range from Hawkins's contemporaries (Garvin Bushell, Happy Caldwell, Sonny Greer, Jacques Butler) to later players and interviewers (Kenny Burrell, JJ Johnson, Charles Lloyd). The stories are set mostly between the 1920s and early 1960s, in New York, Kansas City, Europe and Los Angeles.
