They recall Hawkins arriving with Mamie Smith and Fletcher Henderson, the sound and harmonic sense of 'Body and Soul', his kindness and loner's dignity, and the respect he commanded. Around him are comparable figures: Benny Carter, Ben Webster, Lester Young and Johnny Hodges, named as idols, models or players who cannot be duplicated. The tellers agree Hawkins made the tenor saxophone respectable and was the father of tenor soloists. They differ on who influenced whom (Carter's influence on Hawkins) and on which player each admired as a model. A smaller share of segments drifts to other saxophonists such as baritone players, bootin' tenors and Hans Koller.

communities.name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections tell the story of making a living in the commercial studios, mostly in New York and secondarily in Los Angeles, from the 1950s into the 1980s. The central figures are session players, arrangers and singers who did record dates, network staff work at ABC, CBS and NBC, and above all advertising jingles. They describe how work was booked through contractors, midnight phone calls and answering services like Radio Registry. They also describe three-hour sessions with overtime, union scale, residuals and usage periods, and the ad agency clients who could not say what they wanted. A recurring theme is the closed circle of roughly three hundred musicians who got most of the work, and how Black players were admitted late. Tellers agree the work paid well and demanded sight-reading and versatility, but differ on its worth: some defend it as an ethical need to support a family, while others (Ernie Watts, Herb Ellis, Dave Liebman, Bobby Shew) say it taught craft but starved the spirit, or chose to leave it. Arrangers and composers such as Chico Hamilton, David Spinozza and John LaBarbera tell the writing side of the jingle business.

communities.name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band
communities.narrative: New Orleans musicians, mostly interviewed at Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, remember Chris Kelly, the trumpeter who led one of the city's busiest dance bands in the 1910s and 1920s and died in 1928. Nearly everyone starts with his sound. He was a country-style blues player who used a plunger, a wah-wah mute and sometimes a derby or hat, and he was best known for Careless Love. Others tell how his band worked: house dances, halls such as the Bulls Club and Economy Hall, advertising wagons, and jobs on the Mississippi coast. They list the banjo, guitar, drum and clarinet players he used, and describe a six- or seven-piece group. Kelly could not read music, which is mentioned more than once. Many tellers, including Kid Howard, Earl Humphrey, Harrison Barnes, Peter LaCaze and Jim Robinson, sat in for him, and they disagree about his reliability. Some praise his pay and his tone, while others describe him double-booking jobs, sending substitutes, paying in whiskey, or losing work to rival bands such as Buddy Petit's, Sam Morgan's, Kid Rena's and Jack Carey's. A few samples drift off to other subjects, including Chris Kenner, Charlie Creath and a Leonce band.

communities.name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline
communities.narrative: This community gathers the many musicians and New Orleans neighbors who remember Joe "King" Oliver, told in scattered anecdotes from over a hundred interviews, mostly in the Tulane and Rutgers collections. The stories run from his boyhood and young manhood in New Orleans (about 1900 to 1917): working as a butler or on the riverfront, learning dance music and sight-reading, playing with the Eagle Band and the Magazine Street crowd, and being heard at Tulane Gym. They follow him to Chicago in the 1920s, where tellers recall him as a funny, easy-going, businesslike bandleader at Lincoln Gardens and the Royal Gardens, and the moment Louis Armstrong left his band. Many accounts then turn to his long decline in the late 1920s and 1930s. Tellers recall the gum disease and lost teeth, his eye, his huge appetite and stomach trouble, the silent front-man role at the Savoy, the poverty and the clam-selling in Savannah, and his death. Most of the contributors knew him personally, but a good number only heard him, heard of him, or knew him from records, and they differ on how good he really was and whether his few recordings do him justice.

communities.name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, New York, Chicago and Paris talk about Sidney Bechet as a person and a player, mostly in short portrait-like segments. The stories run from his boyhood in New Orleans (a cheap flute, a wire-mended clarinet, playing for a dollar a night) through the 1919 European trip with William Marion Cook's Southern Syncopated Orchestra, Harlem and Roseland in the 1920s, the Noble Sissle band and the Blue Note sessions of the 1940s, to his long exile in France and his last engagement at the 1958 Brussels Fair. Tellers agree he was a towering, innovative player who was ahead of his contemporaries, admired and copied by younger men such as Buster Smith and Eddie Barefield, and a blues specialist on clarinet before soprano. They differ on his character: some call him beautiful, a friend, or like a king in Europe, while others describe him as selfish, jealous, reserved, hard to know, furious on the bandstand, and armed with pistols and a Lincoln full of hidden weapons. Tellers include New Orleans Creole contemporaries, Ellington and Armstrong-circle sidemen, Blue Note staff and bandleaders who hired him, and expatriates who visited or sat in with him in Paris and Belgium.

communities.name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns
communities.narrative: Musicians across the Tulane, Rutgers, Hamilton and Smithsonian interviews talk about the instruments in their hands: which horn they bought, who made it, and what it sounds like. The most common story is cornet versus trumpet. Players such as Jimmy McPartland, Muggsy Spanier, Peter Ecklund and Moose Zanco prefer the cornet's rounder, mellower tone and conical bore. Others explain why they moved to trumpet, and early New Orleans players like Papa Jack Laine and Louis Tio recall B-flat and E-flat cornets and high and low pitch. A second strand is the makers and the purchase. Conn, Buescher, King, Martin, Olds, Benge and Selmer come up, along with the stores (Werlein's), prices, theft and loss, and endorsement deals. A third strand is the move to flugelhorn and the flumpet, told by Art Farmer, Clark Terry and Woody Herman, mostly from the 1950s onward. The tellers broadly agree that tone and carrying power matter more than looks. They differ on whether old horns were better, as Vic Dickenson argues. The stories are set mostly between about 1905 and 1970, in New Orleans, Chicago and New York, and the tellers range from early New Orleans players to modern jazz trumpeters. Some segments are about trombones, mellophones and care of the instrument rather than cornets.

communities.name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans trumpeters of the 1910s and 1920s to modern players like Wayne Bergeron and Charles Tolliver describe the body side of playing a horn: embouchure, lip placement, breathing from the diaphragm, and keeping the mouth in working order. The stories are practical and often anecdotal. Punch Miller demonstrates how Buddy Petit, Celestin and Kid Punch seated the horn on the lip, and Ernie Cagnolatti recalls Metoyer's rules about centered lips, non-pressure playing, and caring for teeth. Others cover the costs and injuries: sore, cracked or swollen lips, cold sores and lip corns, and dental bridges and caps for players such as Harry Edison and Sandy Williams. A second strand covers technique built on that foundation, including daily scales and mouthpiece practice, double and triple tonguing, flutter tongue, growl and vibrato, half-valve effects, high-note range and breath control. Early New Orleans players tell it as lore handed down from teachers and elders like Perkins, Nelson and Metoyer, and later players tell it as personal routine, equipment choice and health. They largely agree that lip muscle, light pressure and breath from the stomach matter more than force. Trombone, tuba, clarinet and even vocal examples appear at the edges, but trumpet and cornet dominate.

communities.name: Critics, polls and the jazz press
communities.narrative: Musicians across the collections talk about the people who wrote about them: reviewers, record-guide authors, historians and poll organizers. Most of the stories are set between the 1940s and the 1990s, with a few later voices such as the Marsalis brothers, Jane Monheit and Scott Yanow. The sharpest episode is Art Hodes's account of the 1940s "jazz war", when Leonard Feather and Barry Ulanov attacked traditional jazz. Hodes sued Feather for defamation and Feather settled. Other tellers recall single reviews that made or hurt a career. Buddy Tate remembers George Frazier's praise in Boston, and Teddy Wilson calls Frazier a parasite. John Simmons lost an Esquire award after Feather panned his records, and Helen Humes recalls Henry Pleasants's late-career praise. Several musicians complain about being ignored or misdescribed: John Collins is missing from the jazz books, Gene Ramey says McShann and Hines are underrated, and Nick La Rocca feuds with historians. Yusef Lateef, James Moody and Hodes dismiss polls and Down Beat ratings, while Jon Hendricks, Mingus and Steve Wilson reflect on what a critic should be. Musicians mostly resent critics, though some, like Hendricks and Marian McPartland, praise Feather. Critics themselves, such as Howard Mandel, Scott Yanow and Greg Thomas, explain their role and their loyalty to readers.

communities.name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals
communities.narrative: Musicians, mostly New Orleans players interviewed by the Hogan Jazz Archive, are asked who the best clarinetists were and answer by naming names and describing tone, style and reading ability. The setting is mainly New Orleans from the 1900s to the 1940s, with side trips to Chicago, New York and St. Louis. The recurring names are George Baquet, Big Eye Louis Nelson, Alphonse Picou, Lorenzo Tio, Johnny Dodds, Jimmie Noone and Georgie Boyd. George Lewis appears both as a favorite and as a figure whose place in history is debated. The tellers largely agree on who mattered but split on taste: Baquet is fiery, loud and sweet by turns, Big Eye Louis is a great band man but a speller rather than a reader, and Picou is rough when young but better than most. Interviewers such as Russell, Allen and Rose steer these answers by asking directly for favorites. A smaller set of Northern revivalist interviews (Frank Chace, Bob Wilber, Bobby Gordon) discusses Chicago and Bechet-era clarinet influence in the same terms.

communities.name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear
communities.narrative: Clarinetists and saxophonists talk shop about the instruments in their hands: which reeds, mouthpieces and horns they use and why. George Lewis insists on his own mouthpiece, cuts and burns his reeds, and compares wood, rubber and metal clarinets; Charlie Holmes calls himself a mouthpiece freak and buys boxes of Rico number twos; Big Nick Nicholas has played Selmers since 1944. Older New Orleans players such as Paul Beaulieu, Israel Gorman and Joseph Thomas describe Albert-system versus Boehm clarinets and embouchure. A second strand, set mostly in the 1910s and 1920s, is the arrival of the saxophone: who played it first, the move from clarinet to tenor or soprano (Barney Bigard, Lorenzo Tio, Doc Cheatham), and the expectation that a saxophonist also carry a clarinet. Tellers also trade views on which horn famous players used (Lester Young's alto and tenor, Bechet's soprano, Cannonball's switch to Selmer). The stories come from New Orleans veterans, swing-era sidemen and later clarinet revivalists, and they agree that equipment is personal and unfussy. They disagree on whether material makes any tonal difference.

communities.name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: This is the large, loosely bounded story of New York as the place a jazz musician goes to make a career, told by interviewees from every collection. Most stories are set between the late 1920s and the early 1970s, with outliers into the 1980s. They run from the decision to go and the trip itself (train, car, Pennsylvania Station, arriving with fifty cents or $75) through finding a room (the YMCA, a Harlem apartment, a friend's family). Then they cover the first gigs and the clubs and hangouts where the work and the learning happened: Harlem's Rhythm Club and Minton's, 52nd Street, Nick's and the Village, Birdland, the Vanguard and Slug's. Older swing and Dixieland players dwell on Harlem and the Street, while bop and later players talk about Birdland, jam sessions and the Latin clubs. The tellers agree that New York was where the record companies, the best players and the work were, and that musicians urged each other to come. They differ on how welcoming or overwhelming it was, and some, like Red Callender and Von Freeman, push back on its mystique. Because the cluster is so large, it also sweeps in many single-venue or single-gig recollections that are only loosely tied to the move itself.

communities.name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the night-life world of early New Orleans, centred on Storyville and its fringes (Basin, Franklin, Rampart, Iberville, Customhouse/Canal) from about 1900 into the 1930s. They describe the physical layout and economy of the places: Tom Anderson's saloons and Annex, Lulu White's mansion, Pete Lala's, the 25 Club with its glass booth and gambling room, honky tonks and barrelhouses, with prices for drinks, the policeman posted in every cabaret, the string bands and pianists who worked there, and the dress and conduct of the women. Many tellers were hired players or delivery boys on the edges of the district, and their accounts agree on who owned which place and where it stood, often correcting each other or the interviewer about locations. Later segments carry the same cabaret-and-club story into Prohibition-era speakeasies and nightclubs (the Tin Roof, Hotsi Totsi, Silver Slipper, Decatur Street spots) and a few parallel scenes elsewhere, such as Atlantic City brothel piano work, Chicago's 35th Street, Watts and Kansas City-area clubs. The Tulane (Hogan) interviews dominate, with Rutgers and Smithsonian contributing the outside-New-Orleans variants. Much of the interviewing is the interviewer pressing for exact locations, owners and details.

communities.name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall working in a nightlife world run or protected by racketeers during Prohibition and the Depression, mostly 1916 to 1940. Chicago dominates, with Al and Ralph Capone, the Grand Terrace syndicate, State Street and the South Side clubs. The Harlem version centers on the Cotton Club, Connie's Inn, and Dutch Schultz, Owney Madden and the numbers racket, and there are scattered echoes from Kansas City, St. Louis, Albany and Los Angeles. Tellers largely agree that mob-owned clubs meant steady work, good pay and generous tips, sometimes alongside bombs, holdups, shooting and playing at gunpoint. Some, like Buster Smith and Milt Hinton, call the gangsters good bosses, while Glover Compton insists Black-owned State Street clubs were not gangster-run. Around this core sit related stories of bootleg liquor, buffet flats, raids, gambling and rough bars, told by bandleaders, sidemen, singers and New Orleans players alike. A few segments about violence, fights or unrelated incidents stray from the central subject.

communities.name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Musicians across the interviews recall the early New Orleans cornet and trumpet kings they heard, played with or only heard about, above all Buddy Petit and Buddy Bolden, with Kid Rena, Freddie Keppard, Chris Kelly, Joe Oliver and the young Louis Armstrong as points of comparison. The setting is mostly New Orleans from about 1900 to the mid-1920s, with some Chicago, where Keppard and Oliver ended up. Tellers describe tone, range, volume, mutes, fingering and repertoire: Petit is remembered as sweet, soft and round-toned, a middle-register and blues player who read no music and led head-arranged bands. Bolden is remembered as loud and powerful, and much of what is said about him is secondhand. Tellers disagree about the legend: Albert Nicholas was unimpressed by Bolden, and Nick La Rocca says the jazz revivalists invented the Bolden stories. They also differ on whether Petit or Rena was the better player, and on how Armstrong compares. The stories come mainly from New Orleans musicians interviewed by the Hogan Jazz Archive, with some from Rutgers. Many of them come from trumpeters comparing styles, such as Punch Miller, Kid Howard and Chester Zardis, while others are childhood memories from people who heard these players in parks, halls and on excursion boats.

communities.name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players
communities.narrative: Across hundreds of interviews, musicians stop to talk about the trumpeters and cornetists they heard, worked beside or rated best. The stories are mostly short appraisals rather than narratives: who had the strongest tone, the highest notes, the loudest horn, the sweetest waltz playing, the most modern harmony. New Orleans tellers (Tulane) run through lineages such as Manuel Perez, Kid Rena, Buddy Petit, Celestin, Wooden Joe and Papa Jack Laine's cornetists, often ranking them against Louis Armstrong. Swing-era and big-band players (Rutgers, Smithsonian) discuss section men and soloists such as Roy Eldridge, Rex Stewart, Paul Webster, Charlie Shavers and Freddie Webster, usually set in the 1920s to 1940s. Regional schools also appear, notably a St. Louis trumpet sound tied to Charlie Creath and Heim mouthpieces. The tellers agree on tone and chops as the measure of a trumpeter, but differ on whether the greats were the pioneers or the modernists. A few later entries reach Dizzy Gillespie, Freddie Hubbard and Woody Shaw.

communities.name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: At the close of their interviews, many musicians turn to the future and list what is coming up: tours, festival and club dates, jazz cruises, new records, commissions, teaching residencies and clinics. The stories are mostly set from the 1990s to the 2020s, though a few reach back to the 1950s through 1970s. They are told by players of every generation, from swing veterans like Sweets Edison, Joe Wilder and George Masso to later figures like Carla Bley, Denny Zeitlin, Hubert Laws, Robert Glasper and Sheryl Bailey. Destinations recur: Europe, Japan, Paris, New York and Los Angeles, plus jazz parties such as Dick Gibson's. Tellers differ in tone. Some are semi-retired and say no more road work, some are busy with several projects at once, and some joke about avoiding practice or fear a year off. A smaller fringe of segments set in earlier decades, such as Carnegie Hall concerts, Newport and the Gibson parties, are loosely attached because they involve concert dates and venues rather than future plans.

communities.name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan
communities.narrative: American (and some British and other) musicians tell what it was like to play overseas, mostly in Europe and increasingly Japan. The stories run from the 1920s and 1930s, when bands such as Sam Wooding's and Willie Lewis's wintered in France and worked seasonal circuits through Egypt and Belgium, through the 1950s and 1960s (Sarah Vaughan in Paris, J.J. Johnson's Scandinavian tour, Elvin Jones with Coltrane, a Melody Maker-era British tour), to Newport and Nice festival packages, State Department-style embassy concerts and Japan trips in the 1960s and 1970s. Tellers recall the practical texture of travel: boat and train crossings, unheated buses and hotels, language problems, food, contracts and bookers, and the clubs and halls they played, such as Ronnie Scott's, the Palladium and Salle Pleyel. They broadly agree that European and Japanese audiences were warm, knowledgeable and respectful, and that subsidized clubs and better treatment contrasted with the United States. They differ in whether the trip was a brief tour, a stay of years, or a career move, and in how the Europeans' own musicians compared. The tellers are mostly working sidemen and bandleaders from the big-band, swing, bebop and New Orleans traditions, along with a few European observers.

communities.name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Across more than 600 interviews, musicians talk about the craft of putting music on paper and into a band's book: composing a tune, arranging for a section or a big band, orchestrating, writing lyrics, and getting a piece credited or published. The stories run from 1920s New Orleans and Chicago bands (copyright certificates, who wrote "Up a Lazy River", Piron and Sincere setting a song) through the swing-era Basie, Ellington and Henderson books (head arrangements built from section riffs, Fletcher Henderson's charts, Tizol's lost tunes) to bop-era and modern players such as Golson, Jimmy Heath, Slide Hampton, Jim Hall, Carla Bley and younger composers on commission. Tellers describe concrete working habits: writing at the piano, by hand or by computer, waiting for an idea, working to deadlines, writing for strings, or drawing on what other players bring. They also define the crafts. Slide Hampton and Manny Albam separate composing, arranging and orchestrating, and some musicians insist they are arrangers, not composers. Swing-era veterans tend to focus on who wrote what and who got the credit or royalties, while later musicians focus on process, originality and sincerity.

communities.name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song
communities.narrative: Musicians across every era tell stories about getting, or not getting, paid for the songs and records they made. The core is royalties and music publishing: small or late checks, flat-fee buyouts, names added to songs by publishers and bandleaders, and lost or unfair record contracts. Swing and New Orleans players (Trummy Young, Eddie Durham, Juan Tizol, Snub Mosley, Earl King, Joe Robichaux) mostly tell it as grievance, often set in the 1930s to 1950s. They describe tunes sold outright, credits taken by others, and arbitration or lawsuits over authorship. Bop and hard bop players of the 1950s and 60s (Benny Golson, Art Farmer, Cedar Walton, Kenny Burrell, Quincy Jones, Hank Jones) tell a more hopeful version. Gigi Gryce and others taught them to keep their own publishing, and they set up companies such as Thank Music and Janhall Music, and they learned the roles of ASCAP, BMI and the Harry Fox Agency. Later voices (Mose Allison, Jack DeJohnette, Bob Haggart, Eric Alexander) describe sampling, covers, revivals and label statements. A smaller strand covers bootleg taping and record-company bargaining, such as Art Rupe's contracts in Cosimo Matassa's account.

communities.name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it
communities.narrative: Across Tulane, Hamilton, Rutgers and Smithsonian interviews, musicians stop to say what the blues is and what it means to jazz. Most tellers treat it as the root or foundation: "anyone who can play the blues can play jazz" (Leonard Phillips), and Jimmie Crawford calls it the test that exposes symphony-trained players who cannot swing. Many define it as feeling, soul and ideas rather than technique, and the interviewers (Woods, Rowe, Newton) often prompt this by asking about emotion versus study. Others trace its origins to spirituals, field and environmental sounds, the Mississippi Delta, Handy, or even Jewish hymns plus African rhythm, and link it forward to rock and roll and British blues. Technical remarks recur too: the keys where blues sit best, twelve-bar versus eight-bar forms, and blues lyrics that rhyme and tell a story. Tellers are mostly speaking in general terms, so the stories have no single period. New Orleans players recall how blues were played in the old days, and one recording sideman says he tired of it and preferred popular music. Players across generations, from Ory and Barnes to Hutcherson and Turré, agree on its centrality, while differing on what counts as the "real" blues.

communities.name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, Chicago, New York, Texas and the Mississippi Delta talk about church and religion as both the root of their music and a source of tension with it. Most stories are set between the 1900s and the 1970s. They recall childhoods in Baptist, Catholic, AME, Apostolic or sanctified congregations, hearing choirs, organists and spirituals before any jazz, and learning an instrument or voice there. A second strand covers the "devil's music" conflict: families and pastors who disapproved of blues and secular playing, and players who say gospel and blues are close cousins. Mary Lou Williams supplies the largest block, telling of her mid-1950s turn to the Catholic church, her confessor Father Woods, her prayer and fasting, and her break from playing before Dizzy Gillespie and others coaxed her back. Others tell of church jobs and jazz masses, Duke Ellington's Sacred Concerts, and the church's place in New Orleans funerals, wakes and parades. Tellers agree that church shaped their sound. They differ on whether it still does: some say it has not affected their playing, others see religion and jazz as in conflict, and a few see them as one.

communities.name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Across about 300 interviews, musicians and their spouses recount how they met their partners, courted, married and sometimes divorced or lost them. The stories run from a 1905 wedding and 1920s arranged or family-introduced matches in New Orleans, through Depression-era courtships conducted on the road, to 1950s-60s marriages made backstage at Birdland or the Howard Theatre, and a few 1970s-80s reflections. Tellers often give exact dates, wedding venues, in-laws' worries about a musician's life, and who introduced them (a bandleader, a singer, a friend's sister). Spouses sometimes speak themselves (Bella Cornish, Ruth Pizzarelli, Teddie Jones), which brings a different view from the musician's. Differences are mainly of era and setting: earlier tellers describe courtship formalities and family arrangement, while later ones describe how road life strained marriage, childcare and separation. The cluster also includes later-life angles, such as multiple marriages, divorce, widowhood and what sustains a musician at home.

communities.name: Talking about my children and grandchildren
communities.narrative: In this community, musicians step away from the bandstand to talk about their own children and grandchildren, usually when an interviewer asks about family life. The tellers come from every collection (Tulane, Hamilton, Smithsonian and Rutgers) and the stories are set from the 1940s to the 2000s, mostly in New York, Florida, California and New Orleans. A large share of the tellers list their children's names, jobs and careers: sons who became trumpeters, bassists, drummers or sound engineers, and daughters who sing, teach or work with horses. Others are asked whether their kids find the job cool, and the answers range from proud, to polite but unimpressed, to deliberately steering them away from the road, as Teddy McRae did with his daughters. Some tellers made music with their children, as Slide Hampton, Charles McPherson and Jay Leonhart did on records, tours and songwriting, while others, such as Mike Wofford, did not push music on them. Grandchildren appear as short closing notes, such as a grandson who took a trumpet but does not play. A few outliers in the set concern other people's families, such as Buddy Bolden's children or Fats Waller's sons, as told by those who knew them.

communities.name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives are asked, or volunteer, what the word "jazz" meant and where the music came from. Most stories are set between roughly 1900 and 1960, and New Orleans dominates, with Chicago, New York, Cuba and Africa as secondary reference points. Tellers recall when they first heard the word (La Rocca in Chicago in 1916, Reb Spikes after World War I, Sam Wooding in the late 1920s), its underworld or sexual connotations, and Duke Ellington's and Basie's dislike of it. Many separate ragtime from jazz and trace a drift from jazz to swing, bop and free jazz. The origin accounts disagree: New Orleans as the sole birthplace (Cahn, Wiggs, Russell, Lala), jazz as played by Black musicians everywhere (Holmes, Natchez), or Texas and Memphis as rivals. Other versions credit Congo Square, work songs, minstrels and spirituals, and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band's claim to the first recording is contested, for example by those who credit James Reese Europe. A further strand argues over labels such as Dixieland, trad, traditional New Orleans, Chicago style and Latin jazz. These are told by New Orleans veterans, revivalists, swing-era players and later modernists alike, usually as opinion rather than as an anecdote.

communities.name: Politics, race and the state of the country
communities.narrative: In this community musicians step outside the music to give their views on politics, race and the condition of the country. Many of the stories are set in the Obama years (2008-2011), when interviewees such as Benny Golson, Jimmy Heath, Ramsey Lewis, Frank Wess and Curtis Fuller talk about the first Black president, the obstruction he met and how much racism persists. Others look back to the civil rights era and earlier: the sit-ins, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King, Max Roach's Freedom Now suite, Paul Robeson, and McCarthy-era pressure on musicians. A later group reacts to events such as September 11, the Trump years, the pandemic and January 6. The tellers are mostly older, established musicians answering an interviewer's open question about current events, and their tone ranges from hopeful (the system's safeguards will hold) to dismayed. They agree that music offers refuge and common humanity, but they differ on how much change is possible and how much race still shapes American life. Some segments drift to related topics such as health-care costs, corporate power and debt relief.

communities.name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: This community gathers stories in which musicians run into the color line while working, mostly between the 1920s and mid-1960s. They are set on Southern tours, in hotels, restaurants, waiting rooms and dance halls, and in Northern clubs and ballrooms with segregated seating or barred Black patrons. Black tellers such as Ron Carter, Etta Jones, Roy Haynes, Buster Smith and Budd Johnson recall refused service, roped-off audiences, police harassment, jail and carrying guns. White bandleaders and sidemen (Artie Shaw, Louie Bellson, Toots Thielemans, Bud Freeman) tell the same story from the other side: Billie Holiday and the freight elevator, Roy Eldridge's treatment, cancelled Southern dates, and passing as Haitian or Cuban to get around hotel rules. Many stories are about mixed bands, such as the Goodman Trio, Hampton and Wilson, and the first integrated bands in a given town, and about how audiences and white musicians reacted. The tellers differ in tone. Some stress hostility and danger, while others, such as Freeman and Steinau, describe musicians as color-blind and the problem as ignorance or misunderstanding. A few stories reach into civil rights activism and later hiring barriers in studios and orchestras.

communities.name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"
communities.narrative: Jazz musicians recall their work as studio sidemen on pop, rock and R&B records, mostly from the 1950s through the early 1980s, with a few later outliers such as Springsteen's Seeger Sessions (2005-06) and Ricky Martin (c. 1999). The setting is nearly always the New York and Los Angeles studio scenes. The tellers are drummers, guitarists, horn players, keyboardists and arrangers who were called in for a few hours, often to overdub a part (guitar fills, brass, tuba, a cowbell, a Syndrum line) onto a track that was already recorded. A recurring note is that they did not know whose record it was or that it would be a hit: Pizzarelli on "The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face", Porrello on "Sweet Caroline", Raph on anonymous rock and roll dates. David Albert Francis, prompted by Milt Hinton, supplies the longest run of stories. He lists hits he drummed on and tells how he shaped the rhythm of "Patricia" and "Love Is Strange". Other tellers focus on a single name-brand session, such as Paul Simon, Steely Dan, John Lennon, Aerosmith, Mick Jagger, Van Morrison or Bacharach. Some stress how quick or odd the session was: twenty minutes, six hours of Syndrum fills, a solo punched in by the producer. Others stress the craft of arranging and producing.

communities.name: Opening the tape: name, birth date and birthplace
communities.narrative: This community is the formulaic start of an oral-history interview, when the interviewer (very often Bill Russell or Dick Allen of the Hogan Jazz Archive) sets up the tape and the musician states his or her name, date of birth and birthplace. Almost all of the stories come from the Tulane collection, with a few from Rutgers and the Smithsonian, and they cover about 270 different interviews. Most speakers were born between the 1880s and 1910s, usually in New Orleans (the Third Ward, Tremé, uptown, Algiers, Carrollton), but others give Louisiana towns such as Laplace, Reserve and Mandeville, or Memphis, Louisville, Mississippi and Missouri. Typical content includes the street or neighborhood of birth, the recording date and address, a spelling of the name, and sometimes a first teacher, an early start on an instrument or a parent's death. Tellers differ in how sure they are of their dates: Joe Thomas relies on a family Bible, and Julius Handy says his real birth year differs from the one on record. The segments are driven by the interview ritual rather than by any single anecdote, so they read as biographical anchoring, not storytelling.

communities.name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live
communities.narrative: In this community, musicians step back from the music to say what they believe about life. The prompt is usually a closing or reflective question from the interviewer, such as what music has taught them, what makes them angry, or how they cope with hardship. The answers are mostly spiritual or ethical: Christian faith (Hubert Laws, Hank Jones, Red Callender, Harry Edison, Earl May), Buddhism and Nichiren practice (Wayne Shorter, Terri Lyne Carrington, Warren Smith), Hindu and metaphysical ideas such as karma and the Gita (Jon Hendricks, Charles Lloyd, Yusef Lateef), and plainer secular codes of respect, realism and positive thinking. Many of the stories are set in no particular year, and the stories that are dated run from the 1960s to the 2020s because they are about outlook rather than events. Tellers agree that attitude, faith or fate shapes what happens to a person and that hardship can be met without bitterness. They differ on whether music itself is moral or spiritual (Laws says it does not govern behavior; Nancy Wilson calls the stage her pulpit) and on whether life is planned or accidental. Elder players, singers and bandleaders from every collection contribute, and a few outliers drift into politics, art and love.

communities.name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards
communities.narrative: Late in their careers, and often at the close of an interview, musicians reflect on receiving honors, above all the NEA Jazz Masters award, along with Grammys, Down Beat recognition, honorary doctorates, Guggenheim fellowships and city keys. Most stories are set between roughly 1990 and 2016, with the telling usually just after the award, though a few reach back to the 1940s Esquire awards or Count Basie's 1977 Kansas City tribute. A recurring scene is the phone call announcing the award: Sheila Jordan and Jamey Aebersold mistake the caller for a telemarketer or salesman, and Nat Hentoff is stunned by the call. Tellers agree that peer recognition matters more than polls or Grammys, and that the award is a welcome acknowledgment while they are still alive. They differ in tone: Lee Konitz contests the word "master", Barry Harris is surprised and thinks it was for his teaching, and Jason Marsalis discusses the controversy over whether he deserved it. Others use the award to credit collaborators or institutions, such as Lorraine Gordon sharing it with Max Gordon, Snooky Young speaking for first trumpet players, and Dan Morgenstern on the early NEA jazz program. Most tellers are NEA-era elders, with advocates and non-performers (Morgenstern, Hentoff, Keepnews, Aebersold) in the mix.

communities.name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant
communities.narrative: These are the closing questions of an oral-history interview, where the interviewer asks the musician to sum up a life in music. The answers are given at the end of long careers and across the whole century, from musicians who started in the 1920s and 1930s to Sonny Rollins at 80 in 2011. The most common answer is that they would do it all again. Woody Herman, Mary Lou Williams, Art Hodes, Andrew Blakeney and Quinn Wilson all say so, and Mary Lou Williams includes the one-nighters and starvation. Others say what music means to them (Benny Golson, Sonny Rollins), how they define success (Rollins, Nancy Wilson), how they hope to be remembered (David Baker, Lee Konitz, Earl Turbinton on the New Orleans Jazz Workshop), or how lucky they were (Golson, Ignacio Berroa, Flip Phillips on the greatest era). A few differ: Buster Smith wishes he had stayed an electrician, Roy Haynes resents going back over hard times, and Terry Gibbs calls music a crutch against pain. The tellers come from every collection, and they include both older New Orleans players and bebop and later-generation musicians.

communities.name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives talk about the business side of putting out records: how they got signed, what labels did or failed to do for them, and who controlled the finished product. The stories run from the 1940s independents and Chess, Blue Note and Mercury in the 1950s, through Atlantic, Strata-East and ECM in the 1960s and 70s, to the CD-era small labels (Arbors, Telarc, Concord-style indies) of the 1990s and 2000s. Tellers broadly agree that majors demand commercial compromise, promote poorly and pay little, while small or self-run labels give freedom but little distribution or money. They differ on whether labels are crooks (Shirley Horn on Steeplechase, George Russell on ECM) or supportive partners (Rebecca Kilgore on Arbors, Charles Lloyd on ECM). A second strand comes from people who moved into production, reissues or label ownership, such as Bill Goodwin, Phil Schaap, Orrin Keepnews' circle, Marian McPartland with Halcyon, and Jerry Gordon with Evidence. Instrumentalists, vocalists, bandleaders and producers all tell versions of it, set mostly between 1950 and 1991.

communities.name: Interview openings: names, dates and tape setup
communities.narrative: This is not a story the musicians tell but the ritual start of the recording. In nearly every segment the interviewer, most often Dick Allen, Bill Russell or Paul Crawford, announces the date and place, tests the microphone or recorder, and asks the interviewee to give his or her name and its spelling or pronunciation. The sessions are mostly Tulane Hogan Jazz Archive interviews from about 1959 to 1967, with a smaller number from Smithsonian and Rutgers series. Most were recorded in New Orleans, at musicians' homes or in the Howard-Tilton Library seminar room, with some recorded elsewhere, such as San Antonio, San Anselmo, St. Louis and Zachary, Louisiana. The samples mostly agree on the routine of introductions, equipment checks and the start of a new reel. They differ in small details: some openings fix the tape after a machine failure, some name others present, and some pick up where an earlier session stopped. A few add a first biographical fact such as a birth date, or the interviewer's purpose, for example a magazine article. The musicians' own stories begin only after this.

communities.name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand
communities.narrative: In this community musicians reflect on the audience as the purpose and partner of the performance. Mostly older and contemporary players, many interviewed in the Hamilton and Smithsonian series, talk about how they reach listeners: reading the room, programming a set on the spot, talking between songs, explaining the music, and telling a story with a set. Many say the player "makes the audience" and that effort should be the same in a small club, a house concert, Jazzmobile or Carnegie Hall. Some stress entertaining and selling the music, with Dizzy Gillespie, Bobby Short, Zoot Sims and Cannonball Adderley as models of engaging showmanship. Others, such as Marilyn Crispell, are sensitive to audience energy but try not to play for it, and a few, such as Buddy DeFranco, play first for the musicians listening. There is disagreement over whether this can be taught, since several say jazz schools do not teach it and that only the bandstand does. The stories are mostly set from the 1940s to the 2020s, including a return to live audiences after the pandemic.

communities.name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology
communities.narrative: Musicians across eras describe what it was physically and practically like to make a record. The earliest tellers (Darnell Howard, Alberta Hunter, Louis Barbarin, Spiegle Willcox, Louis Armstrong on the Oliver band) recall the acoustic era of the 1910s and 1920s: playing into megaphones and big horns, thick wax, a single microphone, drums avoided or barely picked up, and record companies like Victor cutting out hot solos. Swing-era and bebop players (Sonny Greer, Artie Shaw, Harry Edison, Teddy McRae, Jackie McLean) talk about sessions of about three hours, four sides in a date, two-minute 78s, test cuts, playbacks and exacting engineers at places like Liederkranz Hall and Rudy Van Gelder's studio. Later voices from the 1950s to 1990s (Nancy Wilson, Roy McCurdy, Charles Calello, Larry Gold, Bucky Pizzarelli, Jane Monheit, Nicki Parrott) contrast quick live-in-the-room albums with tape reels, four-track recording, splicing and overdubbing. Producers, engineers and label men such as George Avakian, Cosimo Matassa and Mingus on his ideal engineers explain the pressing, plating and tape-editing side. The tellers agree that older sessions were fast, with few takes and everyone in one room. They differ on whether overdubbing and editing improved the music or compromised it.

communities.name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians across eras recall their first time in a recording studio, and the interviewer often pins down the details: which session came first, which tunes were cut, who played, which label released it, and what was paid. The stories run from 1920s New Orleans and Chicago bands (the Tuxedo Band, Kid Ory's 1923 sides, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, Troy Floyd, King Oliver's men) through 1930s and 40s big-band and swing dates and the Petrillo strike, to 1950s and 60s bebop and hard-bop leader dates and even 1970s-80s self-financed albums. Many segments are discographical detective work, with an interviewer reading session data aloud and the musician correcting, confirming or struggling to remember a pianist, a label or a date. Tellers agree that the first session was memorable for nerves, unfamiliar studio conditions or a mentor who got them the job. They differ in how much weight they give it: some, such as Russell Procope, treat records as just another job, while younger players describe it as a milestone. The tellers are mostly sidemen and leaders recorded in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles and New Orleans.

communities.name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship
communities.narrative: Musicians across several generations reflect on how the jazz business no longer works the way it once did. The stories are mostly told from the 1980s through the 2020s, centered on New York and the record industry, though older players such as Teddy Wilson and Artie Shaw look back at the 1930s as a contrast. The recurring complaint is that labels, agents and publicity machinery now make stars overnight, signing young players (the "young lions" after Wynton Marsalis) while overlooking mid-career and older masters. Tellers say this replaced an apprenticeship system in which young musicians learned on the road with elders such as Hinton or Clifford Brown's mentors, and in which artists were once backed rather than packaged. Others describe the squeeze of shrinking studio and session work, streaming, downloads and social-media follower counts, and the pull of rock and pop crossover. Tellers differ in tone, from bitter (ageism, tribute albums, businessmen dividing the music) to wry or resigned, and the cluster includes sidemen, bandleaders, singers, producers and critics.

communities.name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: In this community musicians step back from their own careers and judge the state of jazz: what happened to it when rock and roll arrived, and whether it will last. The older tellers (Dixieland and big-band players such as Ed Polcer, Charlie Barnet, Punch Miller and R.C.H. Smith) recall the 1950s and 60s, when Bill Haley, Elvis and Alan Freed drew away audiences and the dancing public and Dixieland faded from a fashionable fad. Later interviewees, mostly from the 1990s to 2010s, take up the same question in new terms: hip-hop, tribute festivals, jazz education, smooth jazz such as Kenny G, and the lack of radio play for Coltrane. The tellers disagree. Some are hopeful and name younger players they admire, such as Roy Hargrove, Julian Lage, Esperanza Spalding and Anat Cohen. Others say today's players have technique but lack individuality, seasoning or emotion, or that jazz has become a museum of tributes. Many also worry about the market and the media, and Abbey Lincoln criticizes how the industry images young women singers.

communities.name: Opening the interview: introductions, date and place
communities.narrative: This community is the opening of the oral-history session itself, not a story the musicians tell. In nearly every segment an interviewer (most often Anthony Brown, Ken Kimery, Bill Brower or Ted Panken for the Smithsonian NEA Jazz Masters project, and Helen Johnston, Milt Hinton or Bryant DuPre in the Rutgers and other collections) states the date and place, names the participants and funds or project, and greets the interviewee. Sessions are set in musicians' homes, hotels and clubs from New York, Los Angeles and Washington to New Orleans, Chicago and Fort Lauderdale. Many segments are the start of a second or third day, which resumes where the last session ended. The recordings date from the 1970s Rutgers sessions to Smithsonian interviews through 2012. The tellers rarely differ. The variation is in the formality of the header, whether there is boilerplate and funding credits, and whether the interviewer goes straight to a first biographical question about birth and family.

communities.name: Tape changes, reel headers and session breaks
communities.narrative: This community is almost entirely interview mechanics rather than stories musicians tell. Its segments mark the seams of the recording process: the end of a reel, cassette or tape side, the header for the next one, a break called by the interviewer, or the close of one day's session and the start of the next. They come mostly from the Smithsonian jazz oral history project, Rutgers' Institute of Jazz Studies and Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive. The Smithsonian ones usually carry dated headers, often with Washington, D.C. as the place. Interviewers such as Patricia Willard, Ken Kimery, Hughes, Hinton and Smith announce the changes, and they sometimes recap where the last session left off. Dates run from the 1970s to the 1990s, while the few period tags point to when the interviews were recorded. Interviewees range from Count Basie, Buddy Tate and Maxine Sullivan to Branford Marsalis, and the shape is much the same for all of them. One outlier, Frank Alkyer on a magazine's production cycle, does not belong, and a few segments mix a tape pause with a prompt to return to a topic.

communities.name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection, mostly later-career players and educators interviewed in the Hamilton Fillius series, answer the same question: what goes on in your head when you improvise, and what counts as a mistake? The most common answer is that there are no wrong notes, only notes that are badly resolved or badly treated. Players such as Mike Longo, Wendell Harrison, Bill Dobbins and Chuck Lamb say a clashing note becomes right through the line that follows it. Others, such as Rick Montalbano, prefer the phrase "better choices", and Carmen Lundy says a wrong lyric is harder to recover from than a wrong note. A second strand describes the mental state itself: thinking of nothing, a trance, "the zone", surrendering to the music, with the analytical work done beforehand through learning tunes like a neighbourhood, practising modes, or thinking in larger units. A third strand is advice to students: leave space, play fewer notes, tell a story, favour feeling and melody over chops, and play what you hear. Older players such as Benny Carter, Mary Lou Williams and Joe Wilder tell the same story with less theory, stressing restraint, taste, listening to the harmony and building themes.

communities.name: Advice to young musicians starting out
communities.narrative: This community gathers the closing-style counsel that jazz musicians offer to students and aspiring players, usually in answer to an interviewer's question about what they would tell young people. It is overwhelmingly drawn from the Hamilton College Fillius interviews, with smaller contributions from the Smithsonian, Rutgers and Tulane collections, and it is set in the present of each interview rather than in a particular historical period. The tellers broadly agree on a core: love the music and treat it as a passion, practice and keep learning, listen widely, and be humble. They split on how to hedge a career. Some, like Byron Stripling, argue against a safety net, while others, like Tom Malone, Tony Marino and Magnarelli, recommend a degree or teaching as a fallback. Many add practical business counsel such as learning to read, being versatile, knowing publishing, or getting a lawyer. Older players such as Kid Thomas Valentine, Buddy Tate and Clark Terry give simpler maxims, while younger educators and sidemen often reflect on a shrinking job market and the pull of technology.

communities.name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about teaching jazz: how they came to it, what they do in the classroom, and what they think of jazz education as an institution. Most of the stories are set between the 1960s and the 2010s. Many of the tellers are working players who moved into faculty jobs at Berklee, New England Conservatory, Eastman, The New School, Manhattan School of Music and Juilliard, or into programs like Jazz Mobile. Others teach privately, run youth bands, or play school shows. Several describe being talked into teaching, as Junior Mance was, or drifting into it after leaving a touring band, as Jerry Bergonzi did. They disagree about what schools do to the music. Gunther Schuller describes the prejudice that kept jazz out of education. Ernie Watts and Gary Smulyan worry that academia institutionalizes and homogenizes jazz, and Clark Terry criticizes the educators' association IAJE. Others, like Nat Hentoff and Sam Jones, welcome musicians teaching in schools and want jazz taught from elementary grades. Traditional-jazz players complain that universities teach bebop and big band and neglect older styles.

communities.name: Closing the interview: thanks, goodbyes and tape running out
communities.narrative: This community gathers the final moments of oral-history sessions rather than any story about jazz. Across 270 interviews, mostly from the Tulane Hogan Jazz Archive (with Rutgers, Hamilton and Smithsonian material), the interviewer, often Bill Russell, Dick Allen or Floyd, thanks the musician, notes the time or the tape running out, and ends the recording. Common beats include asking whether anything was left out, arranging a return visit or follow-up call, signing a release form, taking photographs, returning borrowed pictures, and occasionally paying an honorarium. Musicians typically say they have nothing more to add, and a few close with a last remark such as having played with every band in New Orleans or never having recorded. The segments are mostly undated, and the few dates (1959 to 1981) are the years of the interviews, not of the events described. Almost all of the segmenter's own labels call these interview logistics, and the samples agree.

communities.name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview
communities.narrative: This is not a shared story but the ritual end of an interview: the last minutes, when interviewer and musician thank each other and say goodbye. The great majority of the segments come from the Hamilton College Fillius Jazz Archive, where Monk Rowe (and, in earlier sessions, Milt Fillius or a colleague such as Brower) closes the recording, with smaller numbers from Tulane, the Smithsonian and Rutgers. They are mostly undated; where a date shows, the sessions fall between the late 1990s and the 2020s. The closings are usually brief ("Thanks and goodbyes"). Some carry small personal asides: a drive home, a son studying at Eastman, a cab that would not take a bass in the snow, plans to meet at a gig, a question about the YouTube posting, or a remark on how the series affects audiences. A few show the pandemic era, such as Anat Cohen's excitement at playing for audiences again. A handful of off-topic segments (Phoebe Jacobs on the New Orleans airport named for Armstrong, Kid Howard on old clarinetists) are interviews that happen to end in the same segment. The tellers do not differ in substance; what varies is how warm or how digressive the sign-off is.

communities.name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
communities.narrative: Musicians from every region recall how race shaped the town and school they grew up in, mostly in the 1910s through the 1940s. The stories are set in Los Angeles, Detroit, Chicago, Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Dayton, Phoenix, St. Louis, Newark, Boston and small Southern or industrial towns, and they turn on the same concrete details: segregated or "de facto" segregated schools, separate movie theaters, ballparks and swimming classes, the Jim Crow railroad car, Klan-era hostility, and Black neighborhoods such as Dayton's west side. Tellers differ sharply on how bad it was. Some, like Marshall Royal, Eddie Alley and Reb Spikes, remember early Los Angeles or the Western Addition as mixed and barely segregated, and Nick Brignola and Roy Haynes recall multi-ethnic neighborhoods. Others, such as Frank Foster, Clark Terry, Art Farmer and David Baker, describe a daily sense of knowing your place and of schools like Crispus Attucks built to enforce separation. Many also tell how they coped, whether by avoiding trouble, fighting back as boys, or refusing to hate. A few segments drift into boyhood anecdotes (boxing, a motor drome ride, a Creole colorism story) that only loosely touch the theme.

communities.name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they first got a plucked string instrument (guitar, banjo, ukulele, sometimes mandolin or violin) and learned it, mostly in the 1890s through the 1940s. The setting is mainly New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, with Chicago, the Mississippi steamboats and country towns as other settings, plus a few later guitarists from the 1970s. The stories are strikingly similar. A cheap instrument is bought or handed down: $2.75 on Rampart Street, $4 from a neighbour, five dollars at a pawn shop, or a father's gift. There is usually no teacher, so they learn by ear, from a chord book, tuning fork or instruction manual, or from a friend, relative or fellow bandsman. Many then move between instruments (guitar to banjo, ukulele to banjo, guitar to bass) as bands needed them, and a few, such as Kid Ory, built homemade instruments from cigar boxes and buckets. Tellers differ in whether any formal lessons were involved: Souchon and a few others took brief, often unsuccessful lessons, while most were self-taught. They are a mix of New Orleans traditional jazz veterans, blues and R&B players, and later swing and jazz guitarists.

communities.name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians look back on their ordinary schooling, usually before music took over: which schools they attended, how they did in class, and what a particular teacher meant to them. The stories run from about 1900 to the 1960s, with a few from the 1970s and 1990s, and they are set in New Orleans, Chicago, New York, Boston, Los Angeles and small Midwestern and Southern towns. Tellers often describe themselves as good or middling students who liked English or history and ignored math. Many tell of an early exit, such as being expelled after a fight, being pushed out, or quitting to play cabaret shows or to work. Others cover segregated schools and the colleges that excluded Black students, with Wilberforce a recurring destination. Others recall a diploma held back, a late start in school, or the lack of jazz in school music, which was glee clubs and symphonic bands. The cluster is broad and shared across all four archives. It thins at the edges into college and conservatory study (Berklee, Juilliard, Manhattan School of Music, USC) and a few private-teacher stories.

communities.name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons
communities.narrative: Drummers recall how they started: the first kit, how it was acquired, and whether anyone taught them. The stories are set mostly between 1900 and 1949 and are dominated by New Orleans, with Tulane's Hogan Archive supplying the largest share and Rutgers, Hamilton and the Smithsonian adding voices. Early-century tellers such as Jasper Taylor, Alfred Williams, Sammy Penn and Samuel Lovett began on improvised gear (buckets, tubs, cheese-box snares, pots and pans), often copying a brother or following parades and bass drummers. Many insist they never took lessons and learned by watching, while others describe a teacher, a school or industrial-school band, or a professor insisting on solfeggio first. Later and non-New Orleans tellers, from Butch Miles and Jerry Jerome to Sherrie Maricle and Jason Marsalis, tell the same tale with store-bought sets, parental bargaining and school jazz bands. A few, such as Basie, Budd Johnson and Peter LaCaze, say drums were a first instrument they gave up for piano, trombone or trumpet, often because of the bulk of carrying them.

communities.name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from every era and region tell how they came to their first reed instrument, most often a clarinet or saxophone. The stories run from roughly the 1910s to the 1960s, with later players such as Branford Marsalis, Orrin Evans and Adrian Cunningham echoing the same pattern. Relatives are the usual gateway: an uncle hands over or buys the horn (Marshall Royal, James Moody, Orrin Evans), a father starts the child on clarinet (Charlie Gabriel, Spiegle Willcox's account of Gallodoro), or a mother insists on piano or clarinet lessons (Dave Liebman, Lou Donaldson). The other common trigger is hearing a player or seeing an instrument, such as a saxophone in a store window, Johnny Hodges, Benny Goodman on the radio, or Sonny Rollins at a festival. Clarinet frequently comes first as the practical or cheap instrument, with saxophone following, and several tellers started on piano and moved off it. Older New Orleans and Southwest players describe buying on credit, teaching themselves, and learning in school or lodge bands, while younger players dwell on practice, reluctance and teachers. The tellers differ mainly in how much money, formal instruction and family support they had.

communities.name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone
communities.narrative: This community gathers origin stories of how musicians came to their first instrument, with the trombone at the centre and trumpet, cornet and tuba around it. Most stories are set between about 1905 and 1948, in New Orleans, Chicago, New York and small Southern towns. Tellers describe how the instrument arrived: a cheap pawn-shop or junk-store horn, a mail-order trombone, an instrument the school or community band owned, or one a parent or uncle bought on installments. Many were steered to the trombone by a father, teacher or bandleader, or by a shortage of players, or switched to it from cornet, violin, drums or alto horn. Early instruction comes from a neighbour, a school bandmaster or a community-centre band such as the Booker T. Washington Community Center Band, and the first bands and jobs follow quickly. The accounts agree on the accident and economy of starting out. They differ in setting: New Orleans players tell of boys' bands and parade-inspired longing, while Northern and later players tell of high-school bands and private lessons. Interviewees range from New Orleans pioneers to swing-era and bebop-era players, and a few later players such as Jimmy Owens and Ron Carter.

communities.name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, Chicago, big-band and later studio and club settings talk about whether they could read music, and what it cost or gained them. Most stories are set between roughly 1900 and 1950, with many from the 1910s to 1930s New Orleans and Chicago scene (Celestin, Sam Morgan, Piron's boat band, the WPA band). Tellers describe learning to read from method books, from a bandleader or fellow player (Lee Langster, Joe Hooven, Max Fink, Mel Bay), or by following parts on the job. Others recall being exposed or turned down for not reading, as in Barefield's rehearsal, the Suburban Gardens dance number and the Ronica audition. A second strand names great players who did not read, such as Johnny Dodds, Bechet, Armstrong, Ellington, Garner and Wes Montgomery, and argues that feel and ear matter as much. Tellers disagree on the stigma: older New Orleans players often stress that reading got you work, while later players such as Ron Carter, Brubeck and Fred Wesley object to judging jazz players by it. Service bands, theater pit bands and big-band libraries are the settings where reading was non-negotiable.

communities.name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees
communities.narrative: Across more than three hundred interviews, musicians recall how they were first taught their instrument, mostly in the 1910s through the 1930s and above all in New Orleans. The stories name the teacher, often a local professor or brass-band veteran such as Manuel Perez, Papa Tio, Lorenzo Tio, Paul Chaligny, Dave Perkins, Professor Nickerson or Vic Gaspard. They give practical particulars: a quarter, fifty cents or a dollar a lesson, weekly or twice-weekly sessions, and the method books used (Klose, Arban, Otto Langey, a red brass-band book). Tellers agree that early teaching was strict and reading-centred: some teachers withheld the horn for months while pupils learned notes, and others slapped wrong notes or taught counting by foot. They differ on whether they were mostly self-taught with a few lessons or had long formal study. A later strand, from musicians trained in the 1940s through the 1980s, covers conservatory and private study: Juilliard, symphony trombonists, Joe Morello, Slide Hampton and Dave Holland. A few segments show how schooling paid off, such as Cootie Williams's reading getting him the Fletcher Henderson job.

communities.name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening
communities.narrative: Hundreds of musicians recall how they first came to jazz as children and teenagers, almost always through what was playing at home or on the air. The dominant medium is radio: national band hookups and hotel and ballroom remotes in the 1930s and 40s, then disc jockeys and AM and FM stations in the 1950s and 60s. Right behind it come the family record collection, whether a father's Victrola and 78s, a sister's or uncle's albums, or just 45s, and the parents' tastes, which could be swing-minded or entirely non-musical. The bands they name are the Ellington, Basie, Goodman, Lunceford and Calloway orchestras. Younger tellers set in the 1950s and 60s describe Miles, Coltrane and Bill Evans, or rock and roll, R&B and TV scores, arriving alongside or in rebellion against that older music. The tellers agree that listening was their school, and often there was no teacher or local scene at all. They differ in whether jazz came as the family's pop music, as in the 1930s, or as something they had to seek out or even hide from parents. The stories come from musicians of every generation and from all four collections, with many from the Hamilton and Smithsonian interviews.

communities.name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: This is the opening-of-the-interview story: musicians stating who they are and where they come from. Interviewees give their birth date and place, name their parents and grandparents, list brothers and sisters, and describe the house, neighborhood and town they grew up in. It is set mostly between 1900 and the 1950s, across New Orleans, New York, Chicago, Texas, California and smaller Southern and Midwestern towns. The tellers agree on the pattern of the answer, which is names, origins and what the parents did for a living, from cooks and laborers to teachers, seamstresses and florists. They differ on music. Some grew up in musical households with a father on cornet or clarinet, a mother at the piano or in the church choir, or a brother or uncle who played. Others stress that no one in the family played. It is told by musicians of every generation and from all four archives, and it reads as the standard early part of an oral history, with the family told as background before the music begins.
